'''Sugimoto, Cassidy R., Sam Work, Vincent Larivière, and Stefanie Haustein. 2017. “Scholarly Use of Social Media and Altmetrics: A Review of the Literature.” ''Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology'' 68 (9): 2037–62. https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.23833.'''
:Sugimoto et al. review the use of various social media platforms in the scholarly communication process and the alternative metrics derived from their use. They found a high degree of heterogeneity in the literature due to the differences in platforms, methods, samples, and time of analysis, which prevents the generalization of studies on altmetrics and scholarly social media use. Despite these limitations, the authors conclude that social media and altmetrics are more than a passing trend in scholarly communication. However, these platforms do not guarantee broader discussions outside the scientific community, as social media might become a new communication channel among scholars rather than a way to reach the general public.
'''Wixted, Brian, and Catherine Beaudry. 2012. “‘Capturing the Impacts’ of Research: A Discussion Paper Emerging from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council’s ‘Capturing Impacts’ Initiative.” Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2013/crsh-sshrc/CR22-46-2012-eng.pdf.'''
:This report contextualizes and summarizes the findings of 17 impact studies funded through the Social Science and Humanities Research Council’s (SSHRC) Capturing Impact initiative (2006–2007). It categorizes them as discipline-based, knowledge mobilization, and system-level studies. The report’s key finding from the discipline-based studies is that measuring impact in the humanities, arts, and social sciences (HASS) is challenging–in part because of the nature of the research and in part because impact is discipline specific–and developing appropriate metrics is crucial. The key point from the knowledge mobilization studies is that simply producing knowledge does not ensure its use, and determining how and for whom knowledge can effectively be mobilized involves considerable work. The key finding from the theoretical and survey-based system-level studies is that these studies counter the persistent myth that research in the sciences contributes directly to society while HASS contributions do not; measuring these impacts requires qualitative and quantitative approaches, in part because they build over time. The report concludes with a further summary of findings, highlighting the challenge of conducting research due to infrastructural issues, such as the SSHRC’s funding structures and the lack of available and interoperable data.
'''Yang, Siluo, and Mengxue Zheng. 2019. “Performance of Citations and Altmetrics in the Social Sciences and Humanities.” ''Proceedings of the Association for Information Science and Technology'' 56 (1): 326–35. https://doi.org/10.1002/pra2.69.'''
:Yang and Zheng use 1,327,934 Web of Science records and 629,586 altmetric records to analyze the statistical correlation between citation and altmetric indicators in humanities and social sciences (HSS) publications. According to their analysis, there is an especially strong correlation between the altmetric readers count and citations, a relatively strong correlation between the altmetric score and citations, and a weak correlation between citations and other altmetric indices, such as social media, blog, and news mentions. However, the correlations vary by subject field, as psychology had higher citations and altmetric scores, while the arts and humanities had the lowest citation rates and altmetric scores. The findings imply that subject fields in the HSS behave rather consistently between citations and altmetrics, and that altmetric indicators can complement traditional bibliometric analyses. {{Navigation|previous=Introduction|next=Knowledge Mobilization in the Humanities in Practice}} {{BookCat}}

''For the Portuguese version of this introduction, see [https://doi.org/10.25547/N05D-D147 Fundamentos para compreender a Mobilização de Conhecimento nas Humanidades].'' ==Foundations for Understanding Knowledge Mobilization in the HumanitiesSome of the annotations found in this annotated bibliography have been drawn from related work in our research group, namely, published via Open Scholarship Press, Wikibooks, PubPub, Iter Press, and others.== '''Caroline Winter, with Britt Amell''' Knowledge mobilization (KMb) is a broad, complex concept with many overlapping and sometimes conflicting definitions, but it can be understood as the process of putting knowledge to use, within and across the borders of academia and the broader community.For more on terminology related to KMb, see (Colquhoun et al. 2014; Graham et al. 2006; McKibbon et al. 2010; Straus, Tetroe, and Graham 2009). For theories of KMb, see (Graham, Tetroe, and KT Theories Research Group 2007; Rushmer et al. 2019) Many terms are used to refer to the same essential activity of circulating research beyond academia: in the sciences, it is often called “knowledge translation,” which suggests a one-way movement of knowledge from academia to the public in terms that laypeople can understand. It is also often called “knowledge exchange,” which suggests a two-way, reciprocal sharing of knowledge across the academic–public divide. “Knowledge brokers” are intermediaries between researchers and knowledge users.For more about knowledge brokers and knowledge brokerage in the humanities, see (Arbuckle 2020), annotated in this research scan. For more general discussion, see (Auld, Doig, and Bennett 2022; Caswill and Lyall 2013; Knight and Lyall 2013; Meyer, n.d.). ==KMb, An Overview== “Knowledge mobilization” is the most common term in the social sciences and humanities, and it suggests an active, non-hierarchical engagement with knowledge: to mobilize something is to put it in motion, or to put it into action in pursuit of a goal. This research scan uses “knowledge mobilization” because it is the term used most often in relation to the humanities and social sciences and because it captures the idea of putting knowledge into action, echoing the Open Knowledge Foundation’s definition of “open knowledge” as that data that is “useful, usable and used” (Open Knowledge Foundation n.d.). As this connection with “open knowledge” points to, openness is a key facet of knowledge mobilization, since research held within the gated community of subscription journals and pay-to-read databases is limited in its reach. The complexities involved in KMb are compounded when we consider it in a humanities context, since its theories, definitions, and best practices have been largely developed in the sciences, and particularly for the health sciences. Whereas the pipeline from research to practice seems fairly clear in the health sciences, applying KMb theories and practices to mobilizing humanities research is challenging, in part because the nature of humanities research and knowledge is fundamentally different from those of the sciences and the pathways between research and practice are less clear. The pathway from a drug being discovered and tested to being prescribed, makes good sense, for instance, but what is the analogous pathway to use for an interpretation of a poem, or an event in history? How is that kind of knowledge applied, and to what end? Even more challenging are cultural factors, including the belief held by some researchers and members of the broader community alike that humanities knowledge is not useful in the “real world” (see Wickman 2016). Even those who know this knowledge is vitally important may struggle to articulate precisely why or how in a way that is convincing to institutions, funding agencies, and those seeking to defund humanities programs. The widespread resistance within the humanities research community to the instrumentalization and commodification of its work poses another cultural challenge, since KMb efforts may be seen as undermining efforts to advocate for the intrinsic value of humanities knowledge (see Henville 2022). Although articulating the hows and whys of mobilizing humanities knowledge is challenging, it is vital work nonetheless, especially given the institutional contexts in which humanities research is conducted, which often—for better or worse—use research impact metrics as a proxy for research value (Federation for the Humanities and Social Sciences 2014, 10). Quantifying and using metrics to demonstrate the value of the humanities is a particular challenge since, as Joanne Provençal puts it in a study of social sciences and humanities research in Canada, this work suffers from “a paradox of ubiquity and invisibility: present everywhere, but for all intents and purposes, visible almost nowhere” (Provencal 2009, v). Discussing the need for high quality, reliable research from all disciplines to inform public policy, the European Commission points out that communicating findings in a way that policymakers and other stakeholders can understand is essential: “If policymakers cannot comprehend the implications of your work, it will have no policy impact, regardless of its merit” (European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation 2010, 30; see also British Academy 2008). The stuff of the humanities—language, ideas, art, media, history, culture—is all around us in our everyday lives, and because of this its presence and its impact on our lives tends to be taken for granted. One way that humanities research differs from lived experiences of its ‘stuff’ is that research takes a critical view: a researcher analyzing a novel with critical distance experiences it differently and develops a different understanding of it than someone reading for pleasure. This capacity to take a critical perspective and to develop deep, evidence-based understanding and interpretation that characterizes humanities research and the knowledge it generates is an important contribution that the humanities can make to the field of KMb itself, even as they engage in mobilization activities. As Provençal points out,
Knowledge mobilization of research and scholarship to a great extent begins and ends with questions about what “knowledge mobilization” means, and how it is achieved, by whom, for whom, and to what end. […] Along the spectrum between the knowledge broker and community-based researcher, however, there are numerous activities and roles that involve the production and mobilization of knowledge so that the benefits of knowledge can extend ever further. (Provencal 2011, 23)
Along similar lines, in their study of knowledge translation in Indigenous contexts, Bonnie J. Leadbeater, Elizabeth M. Banister, and Anne E. Marshall emphasize the need to understand and name the process of putting knowledge into action as culturally nuanced, arguing that “How-what-is-known-becomes-more-widely-known is context dependent and context sensitive” (Leadbeater, Banister, and Marshall 2011, 5 italics removed; see also Pedersen, Grønvad, and Hvidtfeldt 2020). This relates also to Paul Benneworth’s argument that, “in acquiescing to demands from policy-makers under pressure for clarity and simplicity, a sense of nuance, ambivalence and tensions has been lost from these public debates around the public value of arts and humanities research” (Benneworth 2015, 5). After tracking the history of the so-called, seemingly perpetual crisis in the arts and humanities (see Liu et al. 2022), Benneworth points out that, “whilst social science and humanities researchers might be differently useful to society, their behaviour and orientations do not make them ''a priori'' less useful than science, technology and medicine researchers” (Benneworth 2015, 4–5). In his investigation of the use of bibliometrics for assessing impact in the humanities, A. J. M. Linmans also points to the idea of difference, highlighting the need for impact assessments to consider the lifecycle of the research it is evaluating and how it differs across disciplines. As he notes, “The pace of science is faster and more compact than that of the Humanities, where knowledge develops slower, in spiralling and often erratic patterns. This gives the literature of the Humanities a longer life cycle” (Linmans 2010, 341). What these arguments point to is the need for a recognition of difference in humanities research and knowledge, including difference across disciplines, within fields, between projects, and among individuals who produce and use knowledge. Thinking about KMb in the humanities offers an opportunity not only to critique the institutional and cultural infrastructures that demand quantification of impact as a proxy for value but also to consider critically the nature of humanities research, the knowledge it generates, and its pathway through the world. Indeed, the Federation proposes a definition of research impact that necessitates openness, although it doesn’t call for it explicitly:
Research impact refers to the influence scholarly and creative enquiry has upon wider society, intended as well as unintended, immediate as well as protracted. It includes the influence such research has upon future researchers within the discipline as well as in other disciplines and on public policy, quality of life, social cohesion, business innovation, the environment, artistic and creative practices, commercial and economic activity, administrative and institutional development, and political and cultural understanding.
[…]
“In other words, any definition of research impact must take the long-view of research influence into account as well as the contradictory or inconsistent views of users and reviewers. But research that generates new knowledge both inside and outside universities, research that can improve subsequent research, as well as research that influences the decisions (regardless of outcome) that shape people’s lives, communities, governance, the environment, and elsewhere can be defined as having impact.” (Federation for the Humanities and Social Sciences 2014, 7–9)
Applying the Federation’s broad view of impact, a poem may not be prescribed to treat an illness, but a particular poem may be a staple recitation at weddings or memorial services, or be invoked at times of national crisis—what function, in order words, is it serving? As Brian Wixted and Catherine Beaudry note, “Without knowing how knowledge is used in society, it is hard to improve the practices lying behind its translation from academia to the wider community” (Wixted and Beaudry 2012, 4). That is, to effectively mobilize humanities knowledge, we need to understand what it is and how it moves through the world. ==This Bibliography, A Summary== This research scan is organized into three main sections. Each section presents a curated list of resources and annotations related to knowledge mobilization (KMb) in the humanities. The process for selecting the resources included in this scan consisted of the following iterative steps: (1) carefully reviewing existing bibliographies for potentially relevant resources; (2) searching further for resources using several search terms (namely, “knowledge mobilization” and “humanities,” as well as other related terms such as “knowledge translation,” “research impact,” “social science,” “libraries,” and “public humanities”) and; (3) gathering and reviewing resources in closer detail. During this review stage, resources that focused on KMb in the humanities were generally prioritized over those focusing exclusively on KMb in the social sciences, as were resources that presented case studies of KMb in the humanities in practice. An important aim of this research scan is to support the efforts of those in the humanities to develop shared discipline-specific understandings of the theory and application of KMb. Broad definitions of KMb are frequently featured in assessment and granting frameworks alongside other criteria. Unfortunately, humanities scholars are often left to figure out what knowledge mobilization is or can be, as well as how KMb efforts play out across different contexts and projects—as evidenced in the following lament raised by ‘Anonymous English’ Scholar (quoted in Henville 2022):
I study poetry; my research is not practical, actionable, or quantifiable. In every SSHRC [Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council] application, I make a plan for “knowledge mobilization,” but the truth is that I’m not interested in starting a podcast, and I don’t think there’s a public audience for the poets I study. How do people who don’t do utility-oriented humanities research and write about knowledge mobilization? Or is SSHRC simply not for us anymore?
The resources collected here demonstrate diverse understandings of what it can mean to put humanities knowledge into action. They ask us to think beyond the monograph, essay, or article—and, yes, some resources do utilize podcasts as alternatives to these traditional scholarly outputs. However, the resources in this scan also ask us to reflect more broadly on how knowledge is produced and with whom, as well as the myriad ways in which this knowledge has value within and beyond academia. To illustrate this, the resources found in the opening section of this bibliography (“'''Definitions and Foundations of Knowledge Mobilization in the Humanities'''”) offer a range of overlapping and complementary understandings of KMb that can be drawn on to develop and extend definitions of KMb further. Linking up with current conversations and anxieties regarding the future (or ''futures'') of the humanities, scholarly communication, and the university more generally, this section provokes readers to not only consider the places where principles of KMb overlap with those of open, social, public, digital and engaged scholarship, but to also consider these places of overlap as potential pathways. Rather than one answer, a plurality of responses—along with a plurality of futures in the making—are offered. Lastly, questions about the value of KMb as well as its role in policy development, social change, and innovation are also addressed in this section, as are questions about how (or if) the impact of humanities research can be measured and evaluated using traditional and/or creative methods. The bulk of the bibliography is found in the middle section, '''Knowledge Mobilization in the Humanities in Practice'''. This section, which consists of eight sub-sections, dives deeper into the process of putting humanities knowledge to use. For instance, resources in the ''Community-Engaged Research'' sub-section challenge conventional beliefs about scholarly authority and one-way transmissions of knowledge. In "Antiviolence and Marginalized Communities: Knowledge Creation, Community Mobilization, and Social Justice through a Participatory Archiving Approach" Danielle Allard and Shawna Ferris (2015) investigate methods for facilitating community-led and community-driven engagements with digital archives. At the heart of this work, Allard and Ferris (2015) argue, are at least two commitments. The first is a commitment to anchoring decolonial archival processes in community epistemologies, ontologies, and visions for social justice. The second commitment is an extension of the first, whereby these epistemologies, ontologies, and visions for social justice become encoded in an archive’s organizational framework. They note:
Traditional archives have failed to include forms of Indigenous cultural heritage significant to Indigenous peoples. Indeed, the processes of identifying relevant cultural heritage and constructing it into “archival records” are highly political and have typically excluded Indigenous populations, even when the records in questions have been produced by and/or are about Indigenous peoples. (Allard and Ferris 2018, p. 368)
In seemingly stark contrast, Elizabeth Hoult (2018) grapples with considerations of when ''not'' to collaboratively produce knowledge. “Genuinely co-produced research is underpinned by the commitment to constructing research questions as they emerge around the concerns of the community,” writes Hoult (2018), but “to what extent is it possible to adhere to the principles of a community development approach to co-produced research, when the community involved resides in a prison?” (p. 135). In Hoult’s case, access to community members during the development stage of the research was significantly inhibited by safeguards designed to protect inmates from exploitative academic research. As a result, little to no relationship-building could occur prior to obtaining approval, which seemed to “negate, from the outset, any possibility of co-producing research with the aim of supporting the development of the community” (Hoult 2018, p. 137). Despite this, Hoult concludes that although carrying out truly co-produced research in prison environments may face a number of obstacles, ultimately it is still possible—particularly if an incremental, iterative approach is adopted. The second sub-section, ''GLAM (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums) and Cultural Heritage'', picks up on these threads. It opens with Jon Bath’s and Micheal Peterson’s article on the Shared Spaces project, which aimed to respond to the needs of Saskatchewan arts organizations for digitally mediated ways to engage with art creators and audiences situated across the Canadian province. The authors share how the initial proposal for the project carefully balanced detail with intentional vagueness in order to facilitate and preserve the flexible space needed to engage, from the outset of the project, with members of a diverse arts community. The article follows the trajectory of the project, from the development stage—describing, for instance, steps taken by the project team to ensure communities, including those remotely located, were engaged—to the prototyping stage (a prototyping fest), to the testing and community feedback stage. A number of resources in this sub-section also consider the role libraries play in KMb processes. For instance, Nancy Van House (2003) reminds readers that libraries comprehensively support and foster knowledge creation. Extending this a bit further, authors Sara de Jong and Saskia Wieringa (2014) similarly challenge traditionally held views of libraries and archives as passive storehouses, asserting instead that libraries and archives can be understood as knowledge creators and brokers in their own right (p. 24). Taking a slightly different tack, Emma Wilson and Mary Alexander (2016) argue for the importance of imagining metadata as more than units of information that support the success of digital humanities project (e.g., by making these projects discoverable, navigable, and usable). While the authors still advocate for the importance of high-quality metadata, they also position it as an opportunity for engaging in outreach activities. Sharing examples of the efforts made by librarians and staff at the Alabama Digital Humanities Center (ADHC), Wilson and Alexander build a case for their conclusion that conceptual and applied knowledge about metadata can be meaningfully mobilized through a range of activities, such as consultation and training sessions, other project meetings, and teaching or co-teaching courses across the disciplines. The next two sub-sections, ''Industry Partnerships'' and ''New Media Engagements'', examine different tools and techniques for engaging with partners and audiences across different sectors and platforms. For instance, Amanda Cote and colleagues (2022) share some of the challenges they faced when engaging in research with and about the video-gaming industry. They note that differences in expertise influence needs for different forms of communication, such as in the case of working with developers who are highly skilled at production but perhaps may be less interested in engaging in critique. Relatedly, Cote et al. underscore the value in publishing via non-traditional outlets that developers would be more likely to read (such as Twitch, although GitHub might also be an option). Elsewhere, Kim Martin, Beth Compton, and Ryan Hunt (2017) detail their use of a non-traditional vehicle for KMb—that of a big blue bus, dubbed the ‘DH Makerbus’—to quite literally bring a makerspace, maker technologies, and maker knowledges to wider public spheres. At the same time, they grapple with deeper questions likely to resonate with scholars in the humanities and beyond, such as those that get at the heart of what it means to be and do academic work while also prioritising work that has meaning and benefit for local communities. Martin et al. (2017) also challenge the notion of KMb itself, suggesting that while in theory KMb is often used as a term to describe exchanges of knowledge that are reciprocal, in practice KMb is mostly one directional (Martin et al. 2017). Further, the authors suggest that KMb efforts frequently uphold rather than challenge traditional hierarchies of knowledge production (where academics produce knowledge and community members / members of the public receive or consume information). KMb-related activities, tools, and platforms are emphasized in the latter half of the '''Knowledge Mobilization in the Humanities in Practice''' section of the bibliography. Resources in the Pedagogy sub-section, for example, consider the potential for pedagogical approaches to inform community-engaged research and KMb (e.g., Effinger 2022), as well as the procedural, technical, and infrastructural aspects involved in efforts to enhance the diversity and sense of inclusion among students in the humanities (e.g., Rogers 2020; Sichani et al. 2019). Wikipedia, crowdsourcing, and other methods of facilitating online collaboration are considered in the ''Social Knowledge'' sub-section. Lastly, new(er) opportunities for enhancing the reach, engagement, and exchange of knowledge afforded by new(er) digital technologies and platforms such as Reddit, TikTok, Spotify, and ‘X’ are considered in the ''Podcasting'' and ''Social Media'' sub-sections. The bibliography closes with a further consideration of '''Knowledge Mobilization Resources, Tools, and Guides'''. This section includes a selection of annotated resources related to research communication, impact planning, and data management in the humanities. It also includes an unannotated list of resources related to knowledge mobilization more generally.
***
Across the disciplines, as well as society more generally, there is growing recognition that complex problems (of which there are many) demand complex solutions. Thus, interdisciplinary and cross-sectoral approaches to research and knowledge engagement are urgently needed if we are to address the increasingly frequent challenges, issues, and crises we face locally and globally (Federation for the Humanities and Social Sciences 2014, see also Liu et al. 2022). The humanities have an essential role to play in developing and supporting complex understandings of these problems as well as their solutions. The hope is that the resources shared in this bibliography offer readers a sound place to more confidently engage with and further these and other conversations. As Judith Butler (2022) writes, “the public, the public good, life, and futurity all depend on the humanities,” and “without the humanities, not only is the future itself bleak . . . but we have no way of describing, understanding, or countering that bleakness” (p. 45). The difficult task, however, is making others aware of this dependence. ==Humanities Specific Resources==
'''European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation. 2010. ''Communicating Research for Evidence-Based Policymaking: A Practical Guide for Researchers in Socio-Economic Sciences and Humanities''. https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2777/9276.'''
:This guide outlines best practices for researchers on projects funded through the European Commission’s funding frameworks (e.g., the current one is Horizon 2020), which include objectives related to informing public policy. Noting that high quality research is needed to create evidence-based policy to address the greatest challenges facing the EU, the guide encourages researchers to build policy considerations into their research projects from the beginning. One of the guide’s main recommendations is to create policy briefs that summarize the project’s findings and relevance to key policy issues, and it offers specific advice about the format, structure, and rhetorical strategies researchers should use to communicate their work effectively to policymakers. The guide also suggests that research teams include communicators (such as journalists) and policy makers, and that they use other communication tools such as promotional flyers and brochures, project websites, summary conferences and reports, and media engagements. It concludes by emphasizing that, no matter how significant a project’s findings are, if policymakers cannot understand them, they cannot inform policy development.
'''Hannon, Dewi, Alexis Dewaele, Esther De Smet, and Ann Buysse. 2019. “Guide to Impact Planning.” Accomplissh. Ghent University. https://www.ugent.be/psync/en/projects/impactplanning.pdf.'''
:This guide was created as part of the ACCOMPLISSH project (ACcelerate CO-creation by setting up a Multi-actor PLatform for Impact from Social Sciences and Humanities), a collaboration of universities from across Europe for advancing research impact in the social sciences and humanities. It is intended for researchers and policymakers. It focuses on co-creation, which it defines as stakeholders from the “quadruple helix” of academia, civil society, government, and industry (p. 5) working to solve a common problem and achieving individual goals. In addition to offering an overview of the stakeholder mapping process, it also presents summaries of a variety of research impact planning tools, including online toolkits, training programs, apps, workbooks, and research papers available to researchers.
'''Phipps, David, Krista E. Jensen, Michael Johnny, and Anneliese Poetz. 2016. “Supporting Knowledge Mobilization and Research Impact Strategies in Grant Applications.” ''Journal of Research Administration'' 47 (2): 49–67. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1152268'''
:Most grant applications in Canada, the US, and the UK require knowledge mobilization strategies to support research impact on society, but guidance for researchers in developing these strategies is too general. Therefore, Phipps et al. explore how knowledge brokers can support researchers in drafting strategies to maximize their research impact. They draw on their experiences at York University’s Knowledge Mobilization Unit and the pan-Canadian research network NeuroDevNet to reflect on the different approaches to develop impact strategies depending on the context of the institutions. They found differences in their approaches to training researchers in knowledge mobilization, in the groups they prioritize for outreach, and in the duration of support provided by the units. The authors conclude with a series of recommendations for support professionals and institutions, research administrators, and research funders to improve impact strategies in grant applications.

'''Romary, Laurent. 2012. “Data Management in the Humanities.” ''ERCIM News'' (April). https://ercim-news.ercim.eu/images/stories/EN89/EN89-web.pdf'''
:Romary describes several data management tools in the humanities. ==Community-Engaged Research==
'''Allard, Danielle, and Shawna Ferris. 2015. “Antiviolence and Marginalized Communities: Knowledge Creation, Community Mobilization, and Social Justice through a Participatory Archiving Approach.” ''Library Trends'' 64 (2): 360–83. https://doi.org/10.1353/lib.2015.0043.'''
:Allard and Ferris explain the development of a participatory archiving approach with stakeholder community groups in three digital archives at the University of Manitoba: the Murdered Indigenous Women Database, the Sex Work Database, and the Post-Apology Residential School Database. The scholars and archivists working on these archives involved community stakeholders in both the archival processes of collection development, appraisal and description, as well as in the planning, design, functionality, and appearance of the digital archives. This participatory approach is based on the idea that archives have the potential to support social justice for marginalized populations. To achieve this goal, the authors prioritized building flexible and trusting partnerships with the stakeholder groups of the three archives to discuss the goals and outcomes of the projects and to amplify the activist efforts of these groups.
'''Ball, Sarah, Brandi Leach, Jennifer Bousfield, Pamina Smith, and Sonja Marjanovic. 2021. “Arts-Based Approaches to Public Engagement with Research: Lessons from a Rapid Review.” RAND Corporation. https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA194-1.html.'''
'''Bell, David, Steve Pool, Kim Streets and Natalie Walton, with Kate Pahl. ''“''How Does Arts Practice Inform a Community Development Approach to the Co-production of Research?''.”'' In ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 95–114. Bristol University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.11.'''
:This chapter presents a dialogue between the authors: a researcher (David Bell), an artist (Steve Pool), a chief executive of a museum service (Kim Streets), and an arts educator (Natalie Walton) about how arts can be leveraged to imagine better futures and methods and trends within collaborative research. The first part of the dialogue focuses on the ways arts projects can and cannot empower communities to imagine better futures, with an emphasis on how class influences practices of re-imagining. The second part of the dialogue explores the historical, political, and economic dimensions of community-university partnerships. Central to this conversation is an interrogation of language and terminology. David Bell argues that the word “community” can often serve as a “dog whistle term,” invoking only certain kinds of communities. The chapter concludes by outlining several lessons gathered from the conversation: arts can be used to explore—and reproduce—social tensions, hierarchies, and contradiction; it is at the in-betweenness of conversations that collective knowledge can emerge; and building a more equitable society requires the forces of art, culture, and research, although these forces often get restricted.
'''Burg, Jacob. 2020. “Pedagogy of and for the Public: Imagining the Intersection of Public Humanities and Community Literacy.” ''Community Literacy Journal'' 14 (2): 130–37.'''
:Burg discusses how a pedagogy of and for the public, constructed at the intersection of university and community, implements the digital frameworks and organizational tools of public humanities to enliven practices of community literacy. This type of literacy aims to foster sustainable models of multimodal learning, social justice, and community listening. The author relies on the concepts of concrete utopianism and community listening to refocus the humanist’s work around the cultivation of publics and counterpublics. One way to implement this approach is through new graduate student conferences that expand their audience, are reimagined beyond the university context, and root interactions between organizers, presenters, and the public. Cultivating rooted spaces, Burg concludes, can be a ready-to-hand tool to expand individual and community literacy.
'''Chiles, Prue, Louise Ritchie, and Kate Pahl. 2019. “Co-Designing for a Better Future: Re-Imagining the Modernist Dream at Park Hill, Sheffield.” In ''Co-Producing Research'', edited by Kate Pahl, Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, and Paul Ward, 1st ed., 115–34. A Community Development Approach. Bristol University Press. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.12.'''
'''Gaertner, David. 2017. “Why We Need to Talk About Indigenous Literature and the Digital Humanities.” January 26, 2017. https://novelalliances.com/2017/01/26/indigenous-literature-and-the-digital-humanities/.'''
'''Harte, Liam, and Barry Hazley. 2021. “Creative Writing Workshops and the Narrative Construction of Self: Using Oral History to Explore the Impact of Public Engagement in the Arts and Humanities.” ''The Oral History Review'' 48 (1): 40–58. https://doi.org/10.1080/00940798.2020.1869911.'''
:Harte and Hazley argue that cause-and-effect models of research impact such as the UK’s Research Excellence Framework (REF) are insufficient for evaluating the impact of humanities research. They propose that more nuanced approaches that account for participants’ subjective experiences would represent these impacts more accurately, drawing on a case study about the effects of research-based creative writing workshops. The workshops were part of a project in which participants wrote in response to a research-based play (inspired by a history of Irish literature) centred on themes of Irish migration and diaspora. An initial survey failed to capture the impact of the workshop, so it was followed a few years later by a series of interviews. Participants’ oral histories were analyzed for evidence of how they interpreted and narrated the impact of the experience. The authors conclude by emphasizing that, since research can impact people in complex and indirect ways, analyzing oral histories offers a way to observe how the impact of humanities research emerges and is interpreted over time.
'''Hoult, Elizabeth Chapman. 2018. ‘On Not Doing Co-Produced Research: The Methodological Possibilities and Limitations of Co-Producing Research with Participants in a Prison’. In ''Co-Producing Research'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 135–52. Policy Press. https://doi.org/10.51952/9781447340775.ch007.'''
:Hoult explains her experience conducting co-produced research among a community that resides in prison. The main challenge found is that government and ethics clearance for research in prisons limits the possibility of developing connections with the community so that they can influence the methodology and research questions. Hoult’s study involved several showings of science fiction films to the participants and a qualitative analysis of their discussions about the films, as well as interviews. After hearing the participants’ concerns with being reduced to their crimes, the author proposes that co-produced research in prisons could address this problem by encouraging the participants to create other readings of their lives by writing multiple versions of their futures that challenged the information that was found online about them. For similar future projects, Hoult recommends learning the practices of participants to co-design the study from the start, adjusting to the partner’s timescales, and even working with two separate groups, so the first group can provide their input on the methodology for the second group.
'''Hubbard, Melanie, and Dermot Ryan. 2018. “Digital Humanities as Community Engagement: The Digital Watts Project.” In ''Digital Humanities, Libraries, and Partnerships: A Critical Examination of Labor, Networks, and Community'', edited by Robin Kear and Kate Joranson, 139–47. Cambridge, MA: Chandos Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-102023-4.00010-0'''
:Hubbard and Ryan elaborate how the partnership between a librarian and a faculty member can foster community engagement by students working on a digital public humanities project. They report on the Digital Watts Project, which allowed English students to reflect on the characteristics of a public—as opposed to purely academic—history project. The authors rely on postcolonial and subaltern studies, including the work of Ranajit Guha, as a basis to argue how the narratives and the representation in collections can oppose or reinforce biases and prejudices. The authors close the chapter by highlighting the successful librarian/faculty partnership that got the students thinking about the production of materials as a form of activism against racism, and feeling that they were contributing to the community beyond the university.
'''Leadbeater, Bonnie J., Elizabeth M. Banister, and E. Anne Marshall. 2011. “How-What-We-Know-Becomes-More-Widely-Known Is Context Dependent and Culturally Sensitive.” In ''Knowledge Translation in Context'', edited by Elizabeth M. Banister, Bonnie J. Leadbeater, and E. Anne Marshall, 3–12. Indigenous, Policy, and Community Settings. University of Toronto Press. https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.3138/9781442689961.5.'''
:Leadbeater et al. present a book on context-based knowledge translation efforts that apply research to address health and social issues. The case studies in the book demonstrate that effective knowledge translation requires context-sensitive approaches and infrastructures. Therefore, the studies are organized into sections focusing on the contexts of communities, policymakers, and Indigenous groups. Knowledge mobilization in community contexts is collaborative and facilitates the use of research; knowledge translation in policymaking aims to provide research-based knowledge among other competing sources of knowledge for decision-making; and knowledge translation in Indigenous settings occurs through personal exchanges and community engagement to reconstruct traditional knowledge. These case studies show that knowledge translation is a multidirectional and dynamic process that fundamentally affects the way social and health issues are addressed.
'''Meringolo, Denise D., Lee Boot, Denise Griffin Johnson, and Maureen O’Neill. n.d. “Creating Knowledge with the Public: Disrupting the Expert/Audience Hierarchy.” American Academy of Arts & Sciences. Accessed November 30, 2022. https://www.amacad.org/publication/creating-knowledge-public-disrupting-expertaudience-hierarchy.'''
'''Ostashewski, Marcia. 2020. ‘Studying Singing Storytellers in Cape Breton: Community-Engaged Research-Creation as a Methodology’. In ''The Routledge Companion to Interdisciplinary Studies in Singing, Volume III: Wellbeing''. Routledge.  https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315162546'''
:Ostashewski discusses the Singing Storytellers project, created in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia. This was a public outreach initiative of scholars, artists, and community stakeholders that studied the music and art of bardic traditions through practice-based research that involved singing. The main outcomes of the project were the co-creation of a CD of Ukrainian bardic songs, and a live performance of Malian griots (an oral tradition of epic art). By developing research and creative practice in collaboration with the people who traditionally are the subjects of study, the outcomes are deeply contextualized and attend to the diversity of music and cultures, which transgresses traditional ethnomusicological research. The author defines this research as practice-based, because it looks at music as a tool for change and theoretical praxis rather than an object of study. In addition to the research outcomes, the project led to an increased awareness of the diversity of local communities and their cultures by connecting Ukrainian and African people living in Nova Scotia. ==GLAM (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums) and Cultural Heritage==
'''Bath, Jon, and Michael Peterson. 2020. “Building with the Community: Developing Digital Tools for Engaging with the Arts in Saskatchewan.” ''Pop! Public. Open. Participatory'', no. 2 (October). https://doi.org/10.54590/pop.2020.008.'''
:Bath and Peterson discuss a community-engaged arts research project called Shared Spaces, including their process of community consultation. The project is funded through the Canada Council for the Arts Digital Strategy Fund, which funds transformational projects that support Canadian arts communities in responding to the changing digital world. Shared Spaces began by consulting with arts communities in Saskatchewan to determine their needs, which informed the project’s design. Once funding was awarded, the project team travelled to various communities across the province to gather more information about the challenges they faced; they then held a rapid prototyping hackfest and developed a prototype virtual exhibit using a mobile AR app. They then took that prototype back to the arts communities for further feedback and consultation. The next stage of the project will involve developing a custom AR app and training participants to produce 3D scans of artworks for inclusion in virtual exhibits. The authors emphasize the importance of ongoing community consultation and engagement at all stages of the project.
'''de Jong, Sara, and Saskia Wieringa. 2014. “The Library as Knowledge Broker.” In ''Teaching Gender with Libraries and Archives'', edited by Sara de Jong. Central European University Press.'''
'''Fabian, Carole Ann, Charles D’aniello, Cynthia Tysick, and Michael Morin. 2003. “Multiple Models for Library Outreach Initiatives.” ''The Reference Librarian'' 39 (82): 39–55. https://doi.org/10.1300/J120v39n82_04.'''
'''Greenfield, Briann. 2013. ‘Making the Humanities Public: The Example of Connecticut’s Humanities Council’. ''The Public Historian'' 35 (1): 51–66. https://doi.org/10.1525/tph.2013.35.1.5.'''
:Greenfield traces the history of Connecticut Humanities (CTH), one of the largest humanities state councils in the U.S. in terms of budget and number of staff. In the 1990s, the council lobbied the Connecticut legislature to support its work by arguing that the humanities could increase heritage tourism and generate revenue for the state. While this approach was successful in increasing funding, Greenfield criticizes it for commodifying the public humanities, prioritizing public history over other disciplines, and being unsustainable because of its reliance on inconsistent state funding. After state budget cuts and the 2008 economic crisis, CTH shifted its focus from heritage tourism and advocacy to engaging with community organizations and developing its own cultural programming as ways of reaching local citizens instead of tourists.
'''Kern, Verletta. 2022. ‘Going Public: Library Support for Knowledge Translation and Mobilization for the Public Good’. ''Journal of Library Administration'' 62 (3): 312–33. https://doi.org/10.1080/01930826.2022.2043689.'''
:Kern describes the results of the Going Public symposium organized at the University of Washington to promote and provide training in knowledge translation and mobilization among faculty and graduate students. The four annual Going Public events they organized from 2017 to 2021, all had over 100 participants who expressed interest in knowledge translation and community work to solve problems through public scholarship. Kern argues that libraries can support knowledge mobilization through events such as the Going Public symposium. In turn, libraries can continue with their tradition of bridging academics and the community for the co-production of knowledge.
'''Makula, Amanda Y., and Laura S. Turner. 2022. “Toward Engaged Scholarship: Knowledge Inclusivity and Collaborative Collection Development between Academic Libraries and Archives and Local Public Communities.” ''College & Research Libraries'' 83 (2): 246–277. https://doi.org/10.5860/crl.83.2.246.'''
:Amanda Makula and Laura Turner discuss the role of academic libraries and archives in movements toward more inclusive ways of knowing and community-engaged scholarship. They investigated patterns in more inclusive, community-focused collection development by surveying and interviewing academic librarians and archivists at universities across the United States. Of the 118 survey respondents included in their analysis, 76% indicated that their academic library collects, curates, or preserves materials originating from their local public community. Makula and Turner also found that in community-oriented projects, survey respondents were twice as likely to report working with unpublished archival material as opposed to circulating, or non-archival material. Libraries opening their archives to materials created and/or owned by local public communities is reflective of a broader movement within academia towards including traditionally marginalized perspectives in scholarly projects. Makula and Turner conclude that through integrating locally produced forms of knowledge into academic libraries, universities can create new learning environments for students and faculty and open the academy to those whose knowledge has been traditionally excluded from scholarly conversations.
'''McGrath, Jim. 2020. “Teaching Digital Public Humanities with the Public Library.” In ''Doing Public Humanities'', edited by Susan Smulyan, 39–54. New York: Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003058038-3'''
:McGrath describes digital public humanities in specific contexts to document how digital spaces and tools should vary depending on audiences and objectives. He uses the collaboration between his graduate-level course on digital public humanities and the Providence Public Library as a case study to explore the benefits of approaching digitization and publication through the lens of public humanities. McGrath argues that digital public humanities should require institutions to reassess their approaches to staffing and training, their ideas about labour and expertise, and their methods of collaboration. Furthermore, he encourages public humanities practitioners who are new to digital initiatives to learn from the people, projects, and publications that have been debating the value of public and digital humanities efforts over the last few decades.
'''Ridge, Mia. 2013b. “From Tagging to Theorizing: Deepening Engagement with Cultural Heritage through Crowdsourcing.” ''Curator: The Museum Journal'' 56 (4): 435–50. https://doi.org/10.1111/cura.12046'''
:Ridge reviews the relationship between crowdsourcing and cultural heritage material. She argues that public interaction with a museum or library’s holdings fosters participants’ sustained interest and satisfaction. Ridge surveys crowdsourcing in GLAM institutions (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums), and considers the difference between crowdsourcing and other user-generated content, like survey feedback. She outlines effective techniques for developing crowdsourcing projects, including the integration of games and conscientious design that employs appropriate scaffolding. Ridge underscores the importance of acknowledging crowdsourcing as a public engagement activity, even if the “crowd” and the project initiators never meet face-to-face.
'''Ruffins, Fath Davis. 2022. “Grassroots Museums & the Changing Landscape of the Public Humanities.” ''Daedalus''. https://www.amacad.org/publication/grassroots-museums-changing-landscape-public-humanities.'''
'''Salazar-Porzio, Margaret. 2015. “The Ecology of Arts and Humanities Education: Bridging the Worlds of Universities and Museums.” ''Arts & Humanities in Higher Education'' 14 (3): 274–92. https://doi.org/10.1177/1474022215583949'''
:Margaret Salazar-Porzio discusses the vital importance of museums to the United States of America. She reflects on her own experiences as curator at the National Museum of American History (NMAH)—and those of students and professionals in the field—to emphasize the importance of museums in fostering civic education. This paper may be of interest to policymakers considering museum partnerships or creating arts funding plans, and to those working to foster civic learning. She concludes by saying that, because of their ability to teach civic skills, museums are essential to a democratic society.
'''Van House, Nancy. 2003. “‘Digital Libraries and Collaborative Knowledge Construction.’” In ''Digital Library Use: Social Practice in Design and Evaluation'', edited by A. P. Bishop, B. Buttenfield, and Nancy Van House, 271–96. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.'''
:Van House reminds her readers that libraries are more than just storehouses; libraries comprehensively support and foster knowledge creation. Consequently, she claims, designing and building effective digital libraries depends on a thorough understanding of knowledge work. For Van House, the emergence of digital libraries represents a significant shift in how individuals and communities create knowledge. Digital libraries often foster transgressive, situated, distributed, and social networks of research and knowledge production. Notably, she reinforces the concept that artifacts are not knowledge in and of themselves; knowledge is a complex social phenomenon rooted in contact, daily practice, and partial mediation by artifacts. As such, digital libraries function differently than as mere conduits—digital libraries are boundary objects, and they affect knowledge work significantly by introducing variation in terms of manipulability, credibility, inscription, access, and organization.
'''Wilson, Emma Annette, and Mary Alexander. 2016. “When Metadata Becomes Outreach: Indexing, Describing, and Encoding for DH.” ''Dh+lib'', July. https://acrl.ala.org/dh/2016/07/29/when-metadata-becomes-outreach/.'''
:Although it is widely recognized that metadata librarians have skills that are necessary and in demand for DH projects, Wilson and Alexander argue that this presents an opportunity for metadata to function as a catalyst for new forms of library outreach. To illustrate some of the possibilities, the authors outline three example projects based in the Alabama Digital Humanities Center (ADHC), run by Wilson. These include the indexing of a clothing industry trade publication that includes fabric swatches, the digitization and markup of marginalia in John Stuart Mill’s personal library, and the development of a digital edition of a c. c17–c18 Colombian manuscript with student collaborators. Wilson and Alexander conclude by emphasizing the importance of good metadata to DH projects and the value of collaborations between DH researchers and metadata librarians.
'''Zalta, Edward. 2006. “The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: A University/Library Partnership in Support of Scholarly Communication and Open Access.” College & Research Libraries News 67 (8): 502–4. https://doi.org/10.5860/crln.67.8.7670.'''
:The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP) has been an open access encyclopedia since its inception in 1995, years before open access became a byword in the academic world. In this article, Zalta positions SEP as a model for reform of the scholarly communication ecosystem due to the strength of its university/library partnership, which he sees as a method of supporting principles of reform such as widely available open access research, scholar controlled publishing, reduction of cost, peer review, quality assurance, fair use, and preservation. Zalta argues that SEP provides a model for fair use scholar-led knowledge mobilisation, highlighting its long term global success and broad readership, a readership which includes not only other professionals in the field but also high school students, undergraduates, and the general public. ==Industry Partnerships==
'''Barnett, Tully. 2020. “Public-Private Partnerships and the Digitization of the Textual and Cultural Record.” ''Pop! Public. Open. Participatory'', no. 2 (October). https://popjournal.ca/issue02/barnett.'''
:Writing in the first year of the Covid-19 Pandemic, Tully Barnett provides a critical analysis of the digitization landscape manifesting in public-private partnerships. The article examines a number of such partnerships, highlighting benefits in terms of the funding that is made available to public organizations through partnering and a variety of attendant concerns: putting public documents into private hands, private-sector partners shutting down the products of partnerships, low pay and labour conditions for those working to digitize the world’s cultural material, and public cultural and textual material being used to train AI for private purposes. What emerges is the tension between public and private interests, which has implications for open social scholarship and scholarship in digital spaces more broadly.
'''Cassity, Elizabeth, and Ien Ang. 2006. ‘Humanities–Industry Partnerships and the “Knowledge Society”: The Australian Experience’. ''Minerva'' 44 (1): 47–63. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11024-005-5412-9.'''
:Cassity and Ang examine the experiences of Australian scholars participating in the Australian Research Council’s Linkage Projects between 1998 and 2003, which promoted collaborations between industry and academic researchers, including the humanities and creative arts. The authors found that most academic and industry partners knew each other before working together, and the most common outputs were scholarly publications, followed by less conventional scholarship, such as digital products, exhibitions, and films. However, researchers had fewer collaboration skills and practical pressures than their partners (such as deadlines, budgets, short-term objectives), while the industry partners had to be persuaded of the benefits of research. In this context, the most successful projects involved negotiating the curiosity of researchers and the need for industry outcomes.
'''Cote, Amanda, Kishonna Gray, Christopher Paul, Kelly Bergstrom, Alison Harvey, Christine Tran, and Akil Fletcher. 2022. ‘Studying and Speaking to Industries: A Game Studies Roundtable’. ''Console-Ing Passions 2022'', June. https://stars.library.ucf.edu/cp2022/program/indigo/7.'''
:Cote et al. share the experiences and challenges they have faced when researching and engaging with the videogame industry. To discuss these questions, the scholars draw on their different backgrounds in critical feminist scholarship, black gaming, and decolonial theory, among others. They coincide that when speaking to people in the videogame industry, it is important to write in a clear, short, and accessible way because game developers are trained at production rather than critique. Regarding the teaching of game studies, they mention that the field should broaden the type of work it values and encourage non-traditional research outputs, such as Twitch streams or alternative dissertations. This would foster skills that can be applied not only in the academic industry but in other industries as well.
'''Siemens, Lynne, and the INKE Research Group. 2019. ‘Building and Supporting Humanities-Based University–Industry Partnerships: View from the Academics’. ''Pop! Public. Open. Participatory'', no. 1 (October). https://popjournal.ca/issue01/Siemens.'''
:Siemens explores humanities researchers’ perspectives on the potential, challenges, and outcomes of the Implementing New Knowledge Environments: Networked Open Scholarship partnership between universities, libraries, and academic-adjacent organizations, a project aiming to understand and resolve issues related to digital scholarship in Canada. The participating scholars found challenges in collaborating with others, having differing priorities from industry, and the diversity of the partners making it more complex to move in the same direction. The measures of success were publications, grant funding, tenure and promotion, and improving the implementation of open access. Due to the multiple partners involved in the project, coordination and negotiation is required, but it gives the scholars a larger audience and a practical application to their research, including the possibility to influence policy on open access.
'''Siemens, Lynne and The INKE Research Group. 2019. “Joining Voices: University–Industry Partnerships in the Humanities.” ''KULA: Knowledge Creation, Dissemination, and Preservation Studies'' 3 (1): 15–15. https://doi.org/10.5334/kula.42.'''
:Siemens points out that, although university–industry partnerships are common in the sciences, and their format and processes are understood, this is less true in the humanities. She examines the example of the Implementing New Knowledge Environments: Networked Open Social Scholarship (INKE:NOSS) partnership. Communication is essential for this type and other types of collaboration, including to manage varying expectations, as well as commitment to the project and its goals on both sides. INKE:NOSS is working toward securing a Partnership Grant from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, a program that requires collaboration with industry partners. For this study, Siemens interviewed existing partners. She found that industry partners saw the collaboration as an opportunity to pursue shared interests and work toward common goals. Some challenges included learning about each other’s perspectives and ways of working and the financial and time cost of travel. Since the work was still in progress at the time of writing, Siemens notes that outcomes and benefits have yet to be realized, but this is where disciplinary differences are evident in that they are challenging to quantify and measure. The experience has been positive to this point, however, suggesting that successful university–industry collaboration in the humanities can be achieved. ==New Media Engagements==
'''Balyasnikova, Natalia, and Kedrick James. 2020. “PhoneMe Poetry: Mapping Community in the Digital Age.” ''Engaged Scholars Journal: Community-Engaged Research, Teaching, and Learning'' 6 (2): 107–16.'''
:Balyasnikova and James introduce the PhoneMe initiative, a community-based research creation project designed by University of British Columbia researchers and centred in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside (known as the DTES). The PhoneMe project facilitated the creation and sharing of place-based poetry using a blend of in-person and digital methods. The authors suggest that this project was a worthwhile undertaking as it supported and gave back to the community participants, in contrast to what is known as the ''parachute approach'' when researchers drop into a community to extract research findings and then leave. They also, however, acknowledge the PhoneMe project’s limitation in scope and diversity and outline how they are addressing these issues in subsequent phases.
'''Booth, Paul J. 2015. “Fandom: The Classroom of the Future.” ''Transformative Works and Cultures'' 19 (June). https://doi.org/10.3983/twc.2015.0650.'''
:Booth explores the role fandom can play in the classroom, as it is one of the few places where people can think and write critically after their formal schooling. He argues that the educational system could benefit from more fandom enthusiasm on the part of scholars and students by engaging with fan works and fans themselves in classes, presenting at fan conventions, and writing for fan blogs. These activities are framed in the context of critical fandom, in which fans engage in civil discourse through thoughtful listening and conversation, which are needed for community engagement. Booth concludes that incorporating critical fandom into scholarship can foster collaboration, conversation, and creative thinking in both fan and scholar communities.
'''Bryant, Brantley L. 2010. ''Geoffrey Chaucer Hath a Blog: Medieval Studies and New Media.'' New York: Palgrave Macmillan US. https://doi.org/10.1057/9780230109025.'''
:This edited volume includes a collection of blog posts written in the style of Geoffrey Chaucer that were previously posted online in the 2000s, as well as some reflective essays on the role of blogging in medieval studies. In the essays, the authors agree that blogging can be an informal medium for building community among scholars and the public, reducing the hierarchies of the academic world, and blending medieval scholarship to contemporary pop culture. Another common point is that medievalists are eager users of new digital technologies because scholars tend to humorize their field of study, and their experience with arcane languages such as Latin or Old English facilitates learning the languages used in new media. Given that the Geoffrey Chaucer Hath a Blog website received thousands of hits, Bryant notes that this suggests an interest in medieval scholarship among a diverse audience, a trend that is also reflected in the creation of medieval video games, both of which are a mix of medieval texts and new media.
'''Cortés-Rico, Laura. 2021. ‘Hand in Hand: A Situated Reflection about Knowledge Mobilization between Textile and Digital’. ''Interactions'' 28 (2): 42–47. https://doi.org/10.1145/3449784.'''
:Cortés-Rico describes the Knowledge Dialogues project, an initiative in which Colombian engineering students engaged with local crafters to incorporate design and artisanal perspectives into human–computer interaction practices. These dialogues between students and crafters challenged gender and knowledge boundaries, as engineering is generally associated with the masculine and handmade textiles with the feminine, and scientific knowledge is considered by some as superior to traditional knowledge. The project also changed the traditional engineering approach because the students designed digital–textile interactions with, rather than for, women from their communities. These exchanges made students reflect on their practices by not trying to solve problems, but engaging in a reflective, critical practice that focused on the process instead of the product.
'''Evans, Rebecca. 2017. “Fantastic Futures? Cli-Fi, Climate Justice, and Queer Futurity.” ''Resilience: A Journal of the Environmental Humanities'' 4 (2–3): 94–110. https://doi.org/10.5250/resilience.4.2-3.0094.'''
'''Fong, Deanna, and Mattieu Aubin. 2021. “What Makes Oral Literary History Different?” ''SpokenWeBlog'' (blog). September 7, 2021. https://spokenweb.ca/what-makes-oral-literary-history-different/.'''
'''Harte, Liam. 2017. “Transforming Research into Art: The Making and Staging of My English Tongue, My Irish Heart, a Research-Based Drama about the Irish in Britain.” ''Irish Studies Review'' 25 (1): 71–87. https://doi.org/10.1080/09670882.2016.1266733.'''
'''Hoovestol, Katherine. 2022. “Exporting Shame: Competing Ownership Models in Pirated Transnational Media Flows.” IDEAH, December. https://doi.org/10.21428/f1f23564.f3d46956.'''
:Katherine Hoovestol centres her article on the Norwegian TV show ''Skam'', a piece of media with a large fan base outside Norway, to explore transnational media piracy. Hoovestol argues that producers not only accepted the existence of Skam’s fan base but intentionally promoted fan piracy as a means of translation and promotion . While this made it very effective in reaching its target audience, Norwegian teenagers, the transnational fan base also garnered the interest needed to create a number of spin offs. The paper concludes with the suggestion the producers use of piracy as a method of promotion leads us to questions about affective ownership and the contributions of the fan community in promoting  and translating a media production that then provided profit to its producers without acknowledging the work of the fans themselves.
'''Hurley, Andrew. 2016. “Chasing the Frontiers of Digital Technology: Public History Meets the Digital Divide.” ''The Public Historian'' 38 (1): 69–88. https://doi.org/10.1525/tph.2016.38.1.69.'''
:Hurley questions whether digital technologies have improved public history’s capacity to promote civic engagement in the context of the digital divide. He analyzes the outcomes of a community-engaged project in inner-city St. Louis, where scholars created 3D visualizations of the city from 1850 to 1950. Community engagement with this project was low because it failed to consider the digital divide in online behaviour. In response, the project team blended digital technologies with more traditional public history methods, such as having guided encounters of the visualizations. Hurley concludes that historians should be more cautious about implementing cutting-edge computer applications in public projects for marginalized communities, as they may alienate their intended audiences.
'''Martin, Kim, Beth Compton, and Ryan Hunt. 2017. “Disrupting Dichotomies: Mobilizing Digital Humanities with the MakerBus.” In ''Making Things and Drawing Boundaries: Experiments in the Digital Humanities'', edited by Jentery Sayers, 251–56. University of Minnesota Press. https://doi.org/10.5749/j.ctt1pwt6wq.32.'''
:Martin, Compton, and Hunt discuss the MakerBus that they manage as an example of a project that challenges perceived dichotomies between academics and the public, amateurs and experts. As an independent (not institutionally affiliated) mobile makerspace, the MakerBus brings maker technologies into the broader community, and it is distinct from other similar projects in its inclusion of the humanities, arts, and social sciences in its activities. The authors draw on their academic backgrounds and on their experiences as learners of makerspace techniques and technologies to help build connections with the communities they engage with.
'''Petrarca, Diana, and Janette Hughes. 2014. “Mobilizing Knowledge via Documentary Filmmaking — Is the Academy Ready?” ''McGill Journal of Education / Revue Des Sciences de l’éducation de McGill'' 49 (3): 561–82. https://doi.org/10.7202/1033547ar.'''
'''Research Impact. 2022. ''DOCTalks Connects Across Canada 2022''. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IyquXeGbLVk.'''
:In this panel, four researchers share their experiences creating documentaries for knowledge mobilization as a way of engaging large audiences and creating an emotional connection between the researcher and the people who benefit from the scholarship. The panelists created documentaries on homelessness among older adults, an archaeology project in east Montreal, the creation of Hawaiian Indigenous video games, and the industry of family history and heritage. The speakers agreed that documentary film can be a powerful medium for knowledge mobilization, community building, and advocacy. However, they also warned of the high costs associated with producing a documentary, as it requires hiring professional editors and filmmakers, costs that are challenging to include in traditional grant applications.
'''Rice, Carla, Susan D. Dion, Hannah Fowlie, and Ingrid Mündel. 2022. “Re/Turning the Gaze: Unsettling Settler Logics through Multimedia Storytelling.” ''Feminist Media Studies'' 22 (3): 638–56. https://doi.org/10.1080/14680777.2019.1707256.'''
'''Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. 2023. “The Storytellers.” Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. January 31, 2023. https://www.sshrc-crsh.gc.ca/society-societe/storytellers-jai_une_histoire_a_raconter/index-eng.aspx.'''
'''Van Biljon, Judy. 2020. “Knowledge Mobilization of Human–Computer Interaction for Development Research: Core Issues and Domain Questions.” ''Information Technology for Development'' 26 (3): 551–76. https://doi.org/10.1080/02681102.2020.1767022.'''
'''Vannini, Phillip. 2013. “Popularizing Ethnography: Reflections on Writing for Popular Audiences in Magazines and Blogs.” ''Qualitative Research'' 13 (4): 442–51. https://doi.org/10.1177/1468794113481795.'''
:Vannini describes the process of writing about ethnography in blogs and magazines and offers practical advice for writing pieces for these media. He notes that writing for magazines provides opportunities to communicate a message to a specific audience, to focus more on the informants, and to use multimodal ethnographic data. This type of writing also allows ethnographers to participate in public education, increase the potential of ethnography to produce social change, and give more visibility to fieldwork. Despite these benefits, Vannini warns that writing for popular audiences can lead to misunderstandings and unwarranted criticism from the general public, increase the potential for harm to informants, and cause writers to sensationalize a story to make it more interesting.
'''Virani, Shafique N. 2011. ‘Dissemination and the Digital: The Creation of an Academic Book Trailer’. ''Review of Middle East Studies'' 45 (2): 192–98. https://doi.org/10.1017/S2151348100002421.'''
:Virani proposes the application of digital humanities techniques, especially multimedia, to create academic book trailers that promote scholarly works among the general public. Drawing on his experience creating a trailer for his own monograph in Islamic studies, he argues that creating a book trailer can be less time-consuming than other tasks such as proofreading and the thousands of views his trailer received show that the general public is interested in academic research, especially in formats other than text. Drawing on digital humanities literature that promotes the inclusion of multimedia technologies in research, Virani explains that digital technologies provide new methods for knowledge mobilization, but researchers have been reluctant to use them. This may lead to a gap in the dissemination of knowledge that is usually filled with inaccurate sources of information. ==Pedagogy==
'''Baker, Geoff, and Andrew Fisher. 2013. ''Arts and Humanities Academics in Schools: Mapping the Pedagogical Interface''. London, UNITED KINGDOM: Bloomsbury Publishing Plc. http://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/uvic/detail.action?docID=674914.'''
'''Balleisen, Edward, and Rita Chin. 2022. “The Case for Bringing Experiential Learning into the Humanities.” ''Daedalus''. https://www.amacad.org/publication/case-bringing-experiential-learning-humanities.'''
:Edward Balleisen and Rita Chin respond to concerns about job prospects for humanists and the inward turn of humanists in the United States, pointing out that humanities scholars do more than teach, research, and think: they also exercise soft skills such as communication, leadership, and collaboration. The article draws on initiatives at the University of Michigan and Duke University to explore experiential learning as a method of teaching these skills to satisfy a growing demand to provide preparation for the academic and non-academic job market. Balleison and Chin conclude by calling for increased efforts in curriculum and program evaluation and data collection to support the effectiveness of experiential learning.
'''Clark, Penney, and Ruth Sandwell. 2020. ‘The History Education Network: An Experiment in Knowledge Mobilization’. In ''The Palgrave Handbook of History and Social Studies Education'', edited by Christopher W. Berg and Theodore M. Christou, 253–93. Cham: Springer International Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-37210-1_11.'''
:Clark and Sandwell describe the development and main outcomes of the History Education Network, a Canadian national organization that supported and disseminated research in history education. The goal of the organization was to foster discussions and promote research-informed practice and practice-informed research to history education. For this endeavour, the network obtained funding to build community and mobilize knowledge through conferences, a website, events, and small grant-funded projects. The network, which reached 40 partner organizations, was able to succeed in the long-term because of their strong group of scholars and graduate students committed to the goals of the network, strong communication across disciplines and the country, and strong leadership, factors that other large knowledge mobilization initiatives can replicate if they want to maintain connections among their partners.
'''Effinger, Elizabeth. 2022. “Embracing the ‘Workshop of Filthy Creation’: ''Frankenstein'', Failure, and the Public Humanities.” ''Pedagogy'' 22 (2): 229–52. https://doi.org/10.1215/15314200-9576415.'''
:Effinger describes and reflects upon a public humanities project called Erasing ''Frankenstein'', which brought together women incarcerated in an Ontario prison and undergraduate and graduate students from the University of New Brunswick to create a collaborative exhibit of erasure poetry based on Mary Shelley’s 1818 novel ''Frankenstein''. The project’s knowledge mobilization strategies included co-written presentations at creative writing and academic conferences, a folio of erasure poetry published in a literary journal, three public exhibitions, Effinger’s article and a project website and social media activity. Effinger focuses on the project’s failures in order to model how discussion of failure in the public humanities can be generative. These included challenges to the collaborative authorship model due to institutional structures, lack of adequate time to build community across the incarcerated and non-incarcerated members of the collective, and friction among members. Throughout, Effinger draws connections between the novel’s themes of monstrosity and incarceration and the project, and she concludes by relating the material messiness of the finished poems with the “monstrosity” of the project itself.
'''Estill, Laura. 2017. “Collaborative Knowledge Creation and Student-Led Assignment Design: Wikipedia in the University Literature Class.” ''Digital Humanities Quarterly'' 11 (3). http://www.digitalhumanities.org/dhq/vol/11/3/000320/000320.html'''
:Estill details a case study in which undergraduate students in a third-year Renaissance Drama class use Wikipedia in a literature class. She argues that using Wikipedia can enable students to carry out research using primary and secondary sources, as well as to consider the role of editions and to practice their writing and communication skills—all while working on hypertexts and ontologies. Students also consider the stakes of writing for a real audience that is looking for information, instead of just for the professor who already knows the material. According to Estill, by completing an assignment in this class, students developed a sense of intellectual ownership and learned about collaborative authorship. She also asserts that learning about and analyzing Wikipedia in the classroom can promote digital civic engagement by making digital spaces more inclusive and representative.
'''Jay, Gregory. 2010. “The Engaged Humanities: Principles and Practices of Public Scholarship and Teaching.” ''Journal of Community Engagement and Scholarship'' 3 (1): 51–63. https://doi.org/10.54656/ROWM8434'''
:Jay considers the concept of ''engaged'' or ''community'' scholarship in relation to the humanities. He argues that if the humanities took up such practices, as well as integrated new media tools and techniques more fully, the discipline might gain relevance and public value in an era of funding cuts. The author explains why engaged scholarship has not been as prominent in the humanities as it has in other disciplines: namely, for Jay, the humanities are based on extrapolative, written critique, and this does not translate well to project-based community engagement in the same way that initiatives in the social or medical sciences might. Regardless, Jay sees the rise of social media, digital humanities, and multimodal communication as a promising opportunity for the humanities to increase community engagement around the texts and topics traditionally at the heart of humanistic inquiry. Throughout, Jay is careful to underline the necessity of accountability when it comes to academic / community partnerships, and the importance of avoiding a missionary style of public engagement that the university has often taken on in the past.
'''Jenstad, Janelle, Kim McLean-Fiander, and Kathryn R. McPherseon. 2017. ‘The MoEML Pedagogical Partnership Program’. ''Digital Humanities Quarterly'' 11 (3). https://dspace.library.uvic.ca/handle/1828/9730.'''
