:Jenstad et al. present the pedagogical model for building partnerships between the Map of Early Modern London (MoEML) and digital humanities courses around the world by having students draft content for the project. This model helps ensure the sustainability of digital humanities projects, and provides an opportunity for faculty to meet knowledge mobilization requirements by engaging students in research projects. The model is based on research-based learning, a pedagogical approach where students and instructors address together an unanswered research question. Partnering with an existing project such as the MoEML promotes research-based learning outside of R1 institutions, allows students to contribute to scholarship and share it beyond the scholarly community. The authors conclude that partnership programs such as the MoEML are successful if other projects replicate it to engage students in improving digital resources.
'''Lee, Mia. 2022. “Student-Led Research and Outreach in the Humanities: A Case of Experiential Learning.” ''International Journal of Studies in Education and Science'' 3 (1): 75–84. https://www.ijses.net/index.php/ijses/article/view/20.'''
:Lee describes the creation of a teaching platform based on non-professional history writing that linked student-led university research with secondary school students. In this initiative (developed in partnership with the Singapore Ministry of Education), university students first produced analytical papers on the bicentenary of the 1819 British landing in Singapore and how this related to past issues of migration, resources, and defense and revenue. The students then engaged in experiential learning by synthesizing and digesting their themes and arguments to 13-year-old students in the form of a 40-minute workshop. As another part of the project, the university students mentored groups of 16- and 17-year-old high school students in locating archives, using catalogs, and reading sources. These activities promoted a collaborative, bottom-up approach to history that engaged diverse audiences, inspired an engagement with the past, and broadened the voices typically found in the public school curriculum.
'''Macknish, Cynthia, Tiffany Johnson, and Michael McLelland. 2018. ''Reflecting on Academic Service-Learning Research in a University Intensive English Program''. Brill. https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004392472_010.'''
'''Padrós, Carlos. 2013. ''Teaching Law to Laymen: The Case of the Subject “Law & Culture” in Humanities Studies''. Universitat de Girona. Institut de Ciències de l’Educació Josep Pallach. https://dugi-doc.udg.edu/handle/10256/8309.'''
'''Rogers, Katina. 2020. ''Putting the Humanities PhD to Work: Theory, Practice, and Models for Thriving Beyond the Classroom''. Durham, NC: Duke University Press. https://www.dukeupress.edu/putting-the-humanities-phd-to-work'''
:With graduate education reform as her mission, Rogers argues that current graduate training is not fit for purpose: it primarily trains PhDs to become tenure track faculty members when there are very few tenure track faculty jobs available, and most PhDs end up working in other roles or industries altogether. In doing so, Rogers suggests, academia replicates inequalities since a very small (generally moneyed) sliver of the population is willing to take the risk of such an investment without guaranteed employment upon graduation. She recommends that diversifying academic production modes and outputs would encourage a more diverse graduate student population, and she embraces public engagement activities to this end.
'''Sichani, Anna-Maria, James Baker, Maria José Afanador Llach, and Brandon Walsh. 2019. “Diversity and Inclusion in Digital Scholarship and Pedagogy: The Case of ''The Programming Historian''.” ''Insights'' 32 (1): 16. https://doi.org/10.1629/uksg.465.'''
:Sichiani et al. discuss efforts to internationalize ''The Programming Historian'', which began in 2008 as a hub for open, peer-reviewed tutorials on a variety of digital tools and in 2012 relaunched as an open access, peer reviewed methodology journal of digital history. They discuss efforts to improve its editorial and linguistic diversity and the procedural, technical, and infrastructural challenges involved, including the challenge of working across and embracing cultural differences. The project also emphasizes openness, transparency, and collaboration, such as through open peer review. The authors conclude by noting that, while openness is a key element of The Programming Historian, it does not by itself ensure diversity and inclusion; instead, concerted and ongoing efforts in this direction are needed.
'''Taylor, Laurie N., Poushali Bhadury, Elizabeth Dale, Randi K. Gill-Sadler, Leah Rosenberg, Brian W. Keith, and Prea Persaud. 2018. “Digital Humanities as Public Humanities: Transformative Collaboration in Graduate Education.” In ''Digital Humanities, Libraries, and Partnerships: A Critical Examination of Labor, Networks, and Community'', edited by Robin Kear and Kate Joranson, 31–44. Cambridge, MA: Chandos Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-08-102023-4.00003-3'''
:Taylor et al. present the University of Florida’s perspective on digital humanities programs and practices, which conceptualises them as public humanities. The authors frame the Digital Humanities Graduate Certificate and the Graduate Internship Program as models for both transformative collaboration and engagement of students. They mention case studies of interns who have worked on publishing, sustaining, and translating digital humanities work to emphasize the creative and collaborative aspect of the initiative, as well as the important support it gives to all involved, including students, librarians, and faculty members. They add that as experienced professionals, librarians who work in collaborative practices and with communities are essential partners in their “digital humanities as public humanities” concept. ==Podcasting==
'''Cuffe, Honae H. 2019. “Lend Me Your Ears: The Rise of the History Podcast in Australia.” ''History Australia'' 16 (3): 553–69.'''
:Cuffe examines the role of the history podcast in the Australian context. She glosses a selection of Australian history podcasts—some overtly academic, some not—and concludes that this is an important mechanism for translating historical work (and even historiography) to broader publics. Cuffe acknowledges the challenges of history podcasts in the academic context, namely that there is pushback from those who do not consider knowledge translation worthwhile or intellectually robust, and recognizes that it is difficult to have such work counted in the current metrics-obsessed academic world. Regardless, she still suggests that there is significant value to podcasting, since it both centres a scholarly expert’s voice and invites listeners into the academic process.
'''Johnston, Sonja. 2023. “Bringing Your Humanities Research to Life with Podcasting.” University of Toronto Faculty of Arts & Science. March 9, 2023. https://www.humanities.utoronto.ca/news/bringing-your-humanities-research-life-podcasting.'''
'''Kimbro, Devori, Michael Noschka, and Geoffrey Way. 2019. “Lend Us Your Earbuds: Shakespeare/Podcasting/Poesis.” ''Humanities'' 8 (67): 1–12.'''
:Kimbro, Noschka, and Way ruminate on the relation between podcasts and Shakespeare studies. Not only do the authors suggest that Shakespeare scholars should create podcasts in order to engage with broader publics, but they also consider how the podcast is akin to other emergent, popularizing communication technologies from Shakespeare’s time (like printing) as well as where Shakespeare shows up in current, well-trafficked podcasts. For Kimbro, Noschka, and Way, the connection between Shakespeare and podcasts makes sense from historical, literary, academic, and public engagement perspectives.
'''McGregor, Hannah. 2019. “Yer A Reader, Harry: HP Reread Podcasts as Digital Reading Communities.” ''Journal of Audience and Reception Studies'' 16 (1): 366–89. https://summit.sfu.ca/item/19608'''
:Hannah McGregor explores reread podcasts—a genre of podcast in which the podcasters invite their listeners to reread a favourite book or series with them—as a method of examining space created by new digital fandom environments. McGregor conducted a study of reread podcast listeners, collecting data on their values and experiences. Based on this study, she argues that these podcasts teach audiences to learn to read in a self-reflective manner within their fandom community, potentially teaching the middle-brow virtues of empathy and care and creating a space for analytical exploration of texts outside of the traditional academic landscape. McGregor concludes by calling for further research into these podcasts and fan communities.
'''McGregor, Hannah. 2022. “My Harry Potter Podcast Made Me a Better Scholar.” The Walrus, October 11, 2022. https://thewalrus.ca/my-harry-potter-podcast-made-me-a-better-scholar/.'''
:In this excerpt from ''A Sentimental Education'', Hannah McGregor describes how podcasting taught her the value of bringing her own feelings into her work. Podcasting, she explains, allowed her to explore intimacy and vulnerability in her work in a way traditional scholarship does not support. She looks to scholars Lisa Ruddick and Eve Sedgwick, to examine how academics are taught to suppress their feelings when participating in literary criticism. McGregor describes how the ''Witch, Please'' podcast provided her a space to practise critical feminist methods of literary critique that did not require her to suppress the sadness, joy, and enthusiasm she felt when reading Harry Potter. She describes her own personal growth in response to the community surrounding her podcast and concludes with the suggestion that feminist methods of critique make room for difference in which it is not necessary to understand someone in order to make space for them.
'''Salvati, Andrew. 2015. “Podcasting the Past: Hardcore History, Fandom, and DIY Histories”, ''Journal of Radio & Audio Media'', vol. 22, no. 2, pp. 231-239, https://doi.org/10.1080/19376529.2015.1083375.'''
:Although non-academics do not always engage with academic history, many do engage with history on their own terms as what Roy Rosenzweig has called “popular historymakers.” One such popular historymaker is Dan Carlin, creator of the ''Hardcore History'' podcast. Andrew Salvati compares Carlin’s podcast to long-form documentary and suggests that it is part of a renaissance in long-form nonfiction audio programming. Salvati suggests that the podcast’s popularity is due to Carlin’s willingness to ask more human ‘what if’ questions that draw in what Carlin himself describes as “fans” of history. Furthermore, these fans are supported in their activity by digital technologies, in this case the podcast and its online forums, which have opened new spaces for them to pursue history on their own terms.
'''Thiessen, Janis. 2021. “Canadian History Podcasts.” ''Acadiensis: Journal of the History of the Atlantic Region / Revue d’histoire de La Region Atlantique'' 50 (2): 236–47. https://doi.org/10.1353/aca.2021.0026.'''
:Janis Thiessen's review essay considers 14 history podcasts on Canadian history topics. These podcasts are created by media production companies, organisations and associations, and independent producers. Thiessen draws on analyses by Ira Glass and John Barber to discuss the importance of aural elements and narrative in keeping audience attention. Thiessen emphasizes that most of the 14 podcasts in the article do not use sufficient narrative techniques or use aural elements available to the podcasting medium. Nonetheless Thiessen believes Canadian history podcasts can play a role both as course readings, and as an avenue to reach non-academic audiences, and suggests that podcasts can also be used as assignments in the classroom. ==Social Knowledge Creation==
'''Allison-Cassin, Stacy, and Dan Scott. 2018. “Wikidata: A Platform for Your Library’s Linked Open Data.” ''The Code4Lib Journal'' 40 (May). https://journal.code4lib.org/articles/13424'''
:Allison-Cassin and Scott discuss the possibilities that Wikidata offers in terms of linked open data (LOD) for GLAM institutions (galleries, libraries, archives, and museums), noting that, although the value of linked open data for libraries has long been recognized, technical and infrastructural barriers have stood in the way of widespread engagement. Wikidata, a project of the Wikimedia Foundation, removes many of these barriers as an open platform for creating and using linked open data. The authors provide an overview of how Wikidata works, drawing on their experiences using it, and discuss its applications for community outreach and library systems. They conclude by pointing out that, because Wikidata’s linked open data is created by the community, using it can help address some of the systemic biases built into existing description and metadata structures.
'''Berson, Amber, Monika-Sengul Jones, and Melissa Tamani. 2021. ''Unreliable Guidelines: Reliable Sources and Marginalized Communities in French, English and Spanish Wikipedias.'' Art + Feminism.'''
:Berson, Jones, and Tamani present a report on reliability guidelines for content creation in three Wikipedias: English, French, and Spanish. The authors argue that current reliability guidelines are Western-centric and exclusionary. Moreover, the authors suggest that these guidelines are used to police the boundaries around what is and is not acceptable to include on Wikipedia, to the detriment of marginalized Wikipedia editors. They provide a set of recommendations for reconstruing reliability guidelines in a way that does not replicate colonial and/or exclusionary knowledge creation and authority structures.
'''Bordini, Alessandra, and John Maxwell. 2019. “Breaking SFU Aldines out of the Vaults: Aldus Manutius and Open Social Scholarship in the Sixteenth Century.” ''Pop! Public. Open. Participatory'', no. 1 (October). https://popjournal.ca/issue01/Bordini'''
:Bordini and Maxwell describe Aldus@SFU, a collaborative digitization and open scholarship project commemorating the 500th anniversary of the death of Aldus Manutius (c. 1451–1515), a printer whose innovative efforts to publish and distribute Greek texts continue to inform printing and scholarly practices today. Emphasizing the open and social nature of Manutius’ Aldine Press, the authors draw connections between the challenges he faced and those faced by their own and other digital humanities projects. These include challenges related to collaboration, technology standards, metadata, and preservation. The authors conclude by calling for a re-definition of what makes special collections special: a shift from equating specialness with inaccessibility and exclusivity to equating it with openness and online accessibility.
'''Brown, Susan. 2014. “Scaling Up Collaboration Online: Toward a Collaboratory for Research on Canadian Writing.” ''International Journal of Canadian Studies'' 48 (January): 233–51. https://doi.org/10.3138/ijcs.48.233.'''
:There is a gap in Canada’s infrastructure when it comes to the digital, especially for scholars in the Humanities and Social Sciences. Susan Brownhighlights the lack of national leadership, guidance, and collaboration for the creation of national digital infrastructure. It is difficult, Brown explains, even to find records related to discontinued Canadian government projects except through third party American websites like Google and the Wayback Machine. In the absence of a national plan, Brown puts forward the Canadian Writing Research Collaboratory as a model for the kind of collaborative digital partnership-based infrastructure initiatives that she would like to see. She does not, she says, intend for the Collaboratory to be the only solution to the problem but believes that a number of such initiatives could address the concerningly broad lack of infrastructure facilitating Canadian Humanities and Social Science scholarship.
'''Carletti, Laura, Derek McAuley, Dominic Price, Gabriella Giannachi, and Steve Benford. 2013a. “Digital Humanities and Crowdsourcing: An Exploration.” In ''Museums and the Web 2013'', edited by N. Proctor and R. Cherry. Portland: Museums and the Web. http://hdl.handle.net/10871/17763'''
:Carletti, McAuley, Price, Giannachi, and Benford survey and identify emerging practices in current crowdsourcing projects in the digital humanities. Carletti et al. base their understanding of crowdsourcing on an earlier definition of crowdsourcing as an online, voluntary activity that connects individuals to an initiative via an open call (Estelles-Arolas and Gonzalez-Ladron-de-Guevara 2012). This definition was used to select the case studies for the current research. The researchers found two major trends in the 36 initiatives included in the study: crowdsourcing projects either use the crowd to (a) integrate/enrich/configure existing resources or (b) create/contribute new resources. Generally, crowdsourcing projects asked volunteers to contribute in terms of curating, revising, locating, sharing, documenting, or enriching materials. The 36 initiatives surveyed were divided into three categories in terms of project aims: public engagement, enriching resources, and building resources.
'''Causer, Tim, and Melissa Terras. 2014. “Crowdsourcing Bentham: Beyond the Traditional Boundaries of Academic History.” ''International Journal of Humanities and Arts Computing'' 8 (1): 46–64. https://doi.org/10.3366/ijhac.2014.0119'''
:Causer and Terras reflect on some of the key discoveries that were made in the Transcribe Bentham crowdsourced initiative. Transcribe Bentham was launched with the intention of demonstrating that crowdsourcing can be used successfully for both scholarly work and public engagement by allowing all types of participants to access and explore cultural material. Causer and Terras note that the majority of the work on Transcribe Bentham was undertaken by a small percentage of users, or “super transcribers.” Only 15% of the users have completed any transcription and approximately 66% of those users have transcribed only a single document—leaving a very select number of individuals responsible for the core of the project’s production. The authors illustrate how some of the user transcription has contributed to our understanding of some of Jeremy Bentham’s central values: animal rights, politics, and prison conditions. Overall, Causer and Terras demonstrate how scholarly transcription undertaken by a wide, online audience can uncover essential material.
'''Causer, Tim, Justin Tonra, and Valerie Wallace. 2012. “Transcription Maximized; Expense Minimized? Crowdsourcing and Editing ‘The Collected Works of Jeremy Bentham.’” ''Literary and Linguistic Computing'' 27 (2): 119–37. https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqs004'''
:Causer, Tonra, and Wallace discuss the advantages and disadvantages of user-generated manuscript transcription using the Transcribe Bentham project as a case study. The intention of the project is to engage the public with the thoughts and works of Jeremy Bentham through creating a digital, searchable repository of his manuscript writings. Causer, Tonra, and Wallace preface this article by setting out five key factors the team hoped to assess in terms of the potential benefits of crowdsourcing: cost effectiveness, exploitation, quality control, sustainability, and success. Evidence from the project showcases the great potential for open access TEI-XML transcriptions in creating a long-term, sustainable archive. Additionally, users reported that they were motivated by a sense of contributing to a greater good and/or recognition. In the experience of Transcribe Bentham, crowdsourcing transcription may not have been the cheapest, quickest, or easiest route; the authors argue, however, that projects with a longer time-scale may find this method both self-sufficient and cost-effective.
'''Causer, Tim, and Valerie Wallace. 2012. “Building a Volunteer Community: Results and Findings from ‘Transcribe Bentham.’” ''Digital Humanities Quarterly'' 6 (2). http://digitalhumanities.org:8081/dhq/vol/6/2/000125/000125.html'''
:Causer and Wallace reflect on the experience of generating users and materials for the crowdsourced Transcribe Bentham project. The purpose of the Transcribe Bentham project is to create an open source repository of Jeremy Bentham’s papers that relies on volunteers transcribing the manuscripts. Causer and Wallace argue that crowdsourcing is a viable and effective strategy only if it is well facilitated and gathers a group of willing volunteers. They found that retaining users was just as integral to the success of the project as was recruiting. It was important, therefore, that they build a sense of community through outreach, social media, and reward systems. The number of active users involved in Transcribe Bentham was greatly affected by media publicity. Users reported that friendly competition motivated them to participate, but that an overall lack of time limited their contributions.
'''Crompton, Constance, Lori Antranikian, Ruth Truong, and Paige Maskell. 2020. “Familiar Wikidata: The Case for Building a Data Source We Can Trust.” ''Pop! Public. Open. Participatory'' 2 (October). https://popjournal.ca/issue02/crompton'''
:Crompton, Antranikian, Truon, and Maskell introduce Wikidata as a source of structured humanities data and discuss a case study of its application. They make a case for the value of Wikidata and for humanities researchers to get involved in its development, noting that their expertise is needed to add data about entities as well as the ontological relationships among them. The authors describe their method for extracting biographical data from Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations and contributing it to Wikidata as part of the Linked Familiarity project. They conclude that working with Wikidata is not without its challenges, but that it offers a low-barrier opportunity for humanities researchers to use and create linked open data through open social scholarship.
'''Estellés-Arolas, Enrique, and Fernando González-Ladrón-de-Guevara. 2012. “Towards an Integrated Crowdsourcing Definition.” ''Journal of Information Science'' 38 (2): 189–200. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165551512437638'''
:Estellés-Arolas and González-Ladrón-de-Guevara present an encompassing definition of crowdsourcing, arguing that the flexibility of crowdsourcing is what makes it challenging to define. They demonstrate that, depending on perspective, researchers can have vastly divergent understandings of crowdsourcing. By conducting a detailed study of current understandings of the practice, Estellés-Arolas and González-Ladrón de-Guevara form a global definition that facilitates the distinguishing and formalizing of crowdsourcing activities. Using textual analysis, the authors identify crowdsourcing’s three key elements: the crowd, the initiator, and the process. They advance a comprehensive definition that highlights the individuals, tasks, roles, and returns associated with crowdsourcing. They present a verification table, with nine categories, that can be used to determine whether or not an initiative falls into the classification of crowdsourcing. Estellés-Arolas and González-Ladrón-de-Guevara suggest that further research should be done to understand the relationship between crowdsourcing and other associated concepts, such as outsourcing.
'''Hendery, Rachel, and Jason Gibson. 2019. “Crowdsourcing Downunder.” ''KULA: Knowledge Creation, Dissemination, and Preservation Studies'' 3 (February): 22. https://doi.org/10.5334/kula.52'''
:Rachel Hendery and Jason Gibson discuss the strengths and weaknesses of crowdsourcing projects in the GLAM (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums) sector, taking as their case studies two Australian crowdsourcing projects: the Mapping Print, Charting Enlightenment (MPCE) project and the Howitt and Fison’s Archive (Howitt & Fison) project. They compare Howitt & Fison to the pioneering crowdsourcing project, Transcribe Bentham, and note that in both cases paid transcription labour could have produced a greater output due to the large time investment required for volunteer recruitment, training, and support. The MPCE, however, did target paid academic scholars, but it was found that alternatives, such as automation through machine learning, were more efficient. This is likely because crowdsourcing is not yet seen as legitimate academic labour. Hendry and Gibson argue that, even if most regular contributions are made by a small number of active volunteers, crowdsourcing is a viable method of non-traditional scholarship because Australian funding institutions see it as a means for public impact and engagement.
'''Hiebert, Matthew, William R. Bowen, and Raymond Siemens. 2015. “Implementing a Social Knowledge Creation Environment.” ''Scholarly and Research Communication'' 6 (3). https://doi.org/10.22230/src.2015v6n3a223'''
:Hiebert, Bowen, and Siemens introduce Iter Community, a public-facing web-based platform prototyped by the Electronic Textual Cultures Lab and Iter: Gateway to the Middle Ages and Renaissance, with a specific focus on how this platform is geared toward facilitating social knowledge creation. The authors argue that the emerging area of research known as social knowledge creation promotes critical interventions into the more conventional processes of academic knowledge productions. This type of research is increasingly made more convenient by emerging technologies that allow research groups to more actively participate in and contribute to the dissemination of their work and communication with other partners. The Iter Community page is meant as a critical intervention into modes of scholarly production and publication, and models how the implementation of functionalities that support social knowledge creation can facilitate novel research opportunities and invite scholars and members of the community to participate in the creation of knowledge. The platform facilitates online knowledge production and dissemination in ways that ultimately enhance research practices and community outreach.
'''Jemielniak, Dariusz, and Eduard Aibar. 2016. “Bridging the Gap between Wikipedia and Academia.” ''Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology'' 67 (7): 1773–76. https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.23691'''
:Jemielniak and Aibar consider the relationship between the professoriate and Wikipedia. They recommend that professors become more involved with the open, online encyclopedia. Jemielniak and Aibar cover earlier academic objections to Wikipedia and suggest that many professors do not use the site since they do not see their colleagues use the site. For the authors, engaging with Wikipedia provides a valid and beneficial pedagogical exercise, benefits broader society by improving the quality of information available, and helps to spread one’s research more widely.
'''Manzo, Christina, Geoff Kaufman, Sukdith Punjashitkul, and Mary Flanagan. 2015. “‘By the People, For the People’: Assessing the Value of Crowdsourced, User-Generated Metadata.” ''Digital Humanities Quarterly'' 9 (1): n.p. http://www.digitalhumanities.org/dhq/vol/9/1/000204/000204.html'''
:Manzo, Kaufman, Punjashitkul, and Flanagan make a case for the usefulness of folksonomy tagging when combined with categorical tagging in crowdsourced projects. The authors open with a defense of categorization by arguing that classification systems reflect collection qualities while allowing for efficient retrieval of materials. However, they admit that these positive effects are often diminished by the use of folksonomy tagging, which promotes self-referential and personal task organizing labels. The authors suggest that a mixed system of folksonomic and controlled vocabularies be put into play in order to maximize the benefits of both approaches while minimizing their challenges. This is demonstrated through an empirical experiment in labeling images from the Leslie Jones Collection of the Boston Public Library, followed by evaluating the helpfulness of the tags.
'''Moyle, Martin, Justin Tonra, and Valerie Wallace. 2011. “Manuscript Transcription by Crowdsourcing: Transcribe Bentham.” ''Liber Quarterly'' 20 (3/4): 347–56. https://liberquarterly.eu/article/view/10594/11337'''
:Moyle, Tonra, and Wallace outline the objectives of the Transcribe Bentham project from its initial stages. Transcribe Bentham hopes to harness the power of crowdsourcing to develop an open source repository of Jeremy Bentham’s manuscripts. Beyond digitizing and transcribing the manuscripts, the project aims to create a transcription interface, promote community volunteerism, and roll out a text encoding initiative (TEI) transcription tool, among other things. The authors work through the design concept for the transcription interface and the TEI toolbar, both of which are meant to mask the complexity of the markup. The project team hopes that this initiative will stimulate further public engagement in scholarly archives and that it will introduce Bentham’s work to new audiences.
'''Rockwell, Geoffrey. 2012b. “Crowdsourcing the Humanities: Social Research and Collaboration.” In ''Collaborative Research in the Digital Humanities'', edited by Marilyn Deegan and Willard McCarty, 135–55. Surrey, England: Ashgate Publishing.'''
:Rockwell suggests that crowdsourcing and other community-involved projects offer a path for engaging publics more readily and reasserting the value of the humanities. He argues that regardless of one’s opinion on the role of collaboration in the humanities, scholars need to reconsider the prevalence and value of distributed knowledge, and of projects that purposefully facilitate social knowledge creation. To illustrate his claims, Rockwell provides examples of social knowledge creation projects he has been involved with, including the “Dictionary of Words in the Wild” and the “Day in the Life of the Digital Humanities” (now simply known as “Day of DH”). He nods to other commonly cited crowdsourcing projects like Wikipedia and Transcribe Bentham. Based on his experience, Rockwell offers advice for others undertaking crowdsourcing or social knowledge-based projects.
'''Rosenzweig, Roy. 2006. “Can History Be Open Source? Wikipedia and the Future of the Past.” ''The Journal of American History'' 93 (1): 117–46. https://rrchnm.org/essays/can-history-be-open-source-wikipedia-and-the-future-of-the-past/'''
:Rosenzweig claims that the field of open source software development is notoriously individualistic. He notes that only 6% of over 32,000 scholarly works indexed since 2000 have more than one author, and less than 2% have three or more authors. Rosenzweig argues that the cooperation and freedom of Wikipedia have transformed it into the most important demonstration of the principles of free and open source software movement. He discusses Wikipedia as both a tool for historiography as well as how it can be understood as an expression of history itself. According to the author, professional historians should pay attention to Wikipedia because students do. Wikipedia and Linux demonstrate that there are alternative models to produce encyclopedias and software other than the hierarchical, commercial model represented by Microsoft.
'''Ross, Stephen, Alex Christie, and Jentery Sayers. 2014. “Expert/Crowd-Sourcing for the Linked Modernisms Project.” ''Scholarly and Research Communication'' 5 (4). http://src-online.ca/index.php/src/article/viewFile/186/368'''
:Ross, Christie, and Sayers discuss the creation and evolution of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC)-funded Linked Modernisms Project. The authors demonstrate how the project negotiates the productive study of both individual works and the larger field of cultural modernism through the use of digital, visual, and networked methods. Linked Modernisms employs a four-tier information matrix to accumulate user-generated survey data about modernist materials. The authors argue that the resulting information allows serendipitous encounters with data, and emphasizes discoverability. Linked Modernisms is focused on developing modes of scholarly publication that line up with the dynamic nature of the data and comply with the principles of open access.
'''Saklofske, Jon. 2012. “Fluid Layering: Reimagining Digital Literary Archives Through Dynamic, User-Generated Content.” ''Scholarly and Research Communication'' 3 (4): n.p. https://src-online.ca/index.php/src/article/view/186'''
:Saklofske argues that while the majority of print and digital editions exist as isolated collections of information, changing practices in textual scholarship are moving toward a new model of production. He uses the example of NewRadial, a prototype information visualization application, to showcase the potential of a more active public archive. Specifically, Saklofske focuses on making room for user-generated data that transforms the edition from a static repository into a dynamic and co-developed space. He champions the argument that the digital archive should place user-generated content in a more prominent position through reimagining the archive as a site of critical engagement, dialogue, argument, commentary, and response. In closing, Saklofske poses five open-ended questions to the community at large as a way of kickstarting a conversation regarding the challenges of redesigning the digital archive.
'''Terras, Melissa. 2017. “Crowdsourcing in the Digital Humanities.” In ''A New Companion to Digital Humanities'', edited by Susan Schreibman, Ray Siemens, and John Unsworth, 420–39. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.'''
:Terras explains the role of digital crowdsourcing as a methodology for research on history, culture, heritage, and the humanities in general. She argues that scholars who work in digital humanities should support students who want to become a part of crowdsourcing and create a project in the field of humanities. Moreover, she believes that by encouraging more people to participate in projects related to the humanities we can create a better society that will be more aware of its cultural and social inheritance. Finally, Terras concludes that the development of crowdsourcing in this area can contribute to better access to information about heritage, history, and culture, and that this can, in turn, encourage a wider audience.
'''Vandendorpe, Christian. 2015. “Wikipedia and the Ecosystem of Knowledge.” ''Scholarly and Research Communication'' 6 (3). http://src-online.ca/index.php/src/article/view/201'''
:Vandendorpe argues for the broad uptake of Wikipedia across the academy, contending that researchers need to edit on Wikipedia and to share their specialized knowledge with the rest of the world. In this way, Vandendorpe argues, scholars can easily share their findings broadly and publicly. He emphasizes online, popular, and open access environments in the growing media ecology that supports scholarly communication. Vandendorpe champions the opportunities afforded by serious academic engagement with Wikipedia.
'''Vandendorpe, Christian. 2012. “Wikisource and the Scholarly Book.” ''Scholarly and Research Communication'' 3 (4). https://doi.org/10.22230/src.2012v3n4a58'''
:Vandendorpe contemplates Wikisource, a project of the Wikimedia foundation, as a potential platform for reading and editing scholarly books. He comes to this conclusion after considering what the ideal e-book or digital knowledge environment should look like. For Vandendorpe, this artifact must be available on the web; reflect the metaphor of a forest of knowledge, rather than a container; situate the reader at the centre of the experience; and be open, reliable, robust, and expandable. Wikisource, the author concludes, has the potential to meet these criteria. Vandendorpe highlights that Wikisource enables quality editing and robust versioning, and has various display options. He also outlines areas of development for Wikisource to become an ideal candidate for hosting the aforementioned type of knowledge creation.
'''Walsh, Brandon, Claire Maiers, Gwen Nelly, Jeremy Boggs, and Praxis Program Team. 2014. “Crowdsourcing Individual Interpretations: Between Microtasking and Multitasking.” ''Literary and Linguistic Computing'' 29 (3): 379–86. https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqu030'''
:Walsh, Maiers, Nally, Boggs, et al. track the creation of Prism, an individual text markup tool developed by the Praxis Program at the University of Virginia. Prism was conceived in response to Jerome McGann’s call for textual markup tools that foreground subjectivity, as the tool illustrates how different groups of readers engage with a text. Prism is designed to assist with projects that blend two approaches to crowdsourcing: microtasking and macrotasking. A compelling quality of Prism is that it balances the constraint necessary for generating productive metadata with the flexibility necessary for facilitating social, negotiable interactions with the textual object. In that way, Prism is poised to redefine crowdsourcing in the digital humanities. ==Social Media==
'''Facca, Danica, Arun Jacob, junoh kimm, J. P. King, Mujgan Ozceylan, and Sara M. Grimes. 2022. “Academic TikTok Report.” https://hdl.handle.net/1807/124170.'''
:This report describes the findings of a pilot study to evaluate the use of TikTok as a pedagogical tool for engaging students and as a knowledge mobilization tool for sharing research findings. In order to propose a set of best practices for academics interested in using TikTok for knowledge mobilization, the authors provide background and contextual information about the app, the aesthetics of its content, and information about its user base. They suggest ensuring that the knowledge being mobilized is a good fit for the platform and its user base; keeping videos short, casual and simple; making content accessible through storytelling techniques; and encouraging audience participation. Given that 62% of TikTok users are under the age of 30 and the platform is central to their everyday lives, the authors state that the app can be a tool for educators to connect with students and young stakeholders.
'''Gilbert, Sarah A. 2020. “‘I Run the World’s Largest Historical Outreach Project and It’s on a Cesspool of a Website.’ Moderating a Public Scholarship Site on Reddit: A Case Study of r/AskHistorians.” ''Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction'' 4 (CSCW1): 19:1-19.27. https://doi.org/10.1145/3392822.'''
:Gilbert presents findings of an ethnographic study of r/AskHistorians, a public history initiative in the form of a subreddit on the social media platform Reddit. The subreddit is a place for users to ask questions about history that are answered by experts within the community, and it is more actively moderated than most spaces on the platform, which generally bans illegal or spam content only. Through a case study of a particular question, the responses it received, and the moderation employed to manage the thread, Gilbert shows that, although this moderation is labour intensive and involves some risk to the moderators, applying moderation principles adapted from the academic study of history has made r/AskHistorians an effective venue for public history, not only because it provides reliable answers to users’ questions but also because it models the work of history as well as productive debate. In this way, Gilbert concludes, the work of the subreddit’s volunteer moderators helps to improve users’ information literacy and resist the spread of misinformation.
'''Ross, Claire. 2012. “Social Media for Digital Humanities and Community Engagement.” In ''Digital Humanities in Practice'', edited by Claire Warwick, Melissa Terras, and Julianne Nyhan, 23–46. https://doi.org/10.29085/9781856049054.003'''
:Ross explores the current uses of social media—which she defines as web-based tools that allow community participation, collaboration, and sharing—for digital humanities research. She also reviews the opportunities and challenges of utilizing social media in academia for community engagement, and suggests that the main applications of social media in digital humanities are crowdsourcing, enhancing a community of practice, and co-creating knowledge. The author points out that there is still much to learn about the impact these technologies have on teaching and researching, based on case studies of the University College London, including a project for transcribing Jeremy Bentham’s works by crowdsourcing; the use of Twitter during three digital humanities conferences; and the QRator Project, which allows researchers and visitors of a museum to view and share thoughts and interpretations of each object using QR codes. Ross remarks that to better understand the impact of social media in the academy, universities need to incorporate social media into their approaches to engage communities in scholarly debate and knowledge sharing. {{Navigation|previous=Definitions and Foundations|next=Knowledge Mobilization Resources, Tools, and Guides}} {{BookCat}}

Engaging Knowledge Diversity/Bibliodiver.text:
==Definitions== '''Bibliodiversity''': The degree to which the scholarly communications industry can produce a broad range of publication outputs (e.g., books, journal articles). A publishing ecosystem that is rich in bibliodiversity creates the conditions for a range of ideas to be expressed and enables diverse knowledge producers to contribute their perspectives. '''Lingua Franca''': A bridge language adopted by speakers who do not share a common native language. For example, a person who speaks Spanish and a person who speaks Arabic may use English to communicate with one another. In this case, English would be a lingua franca. ==Resources==
'''Balula, Ana, and Delfim Leão. 2021. “Multilingualism within Scholarly Communication in SSH. A Literature Review.” ''JLIS.It'' 12 (2): 88–98 https://jlis.fupress.net/index.php/jlis/article/view/6'''
:Balula and Leão analyze twelve documents on the key factors that influence language selection and multilingualism in scholarly communication to provide recommendations for future initiatives related to multilingualism in the context of open science. The findings indicate that the use of English as lingua franca facilitates the dissemination of research outputs and breakthroughs to a broader international audience. However, this trend shifts in the social sciences and humanities, where research is often conducted in local languages. The review also addresses the impact of language competence on scholarly communication, noting that different languages shape the way information is conveyed and understood due to cultural nuances. Research not written in English often faces undervaluation, posing challenges for researchers working in their native languages, while producing knowledge in a second language requires navigating different conceptual frameworks. Furthermore, language barriers significantly affect the process of knowledge co-construction, as indicated by the fact that most citations in the reviewed documents were from authors of the same nationality in Central and Eastern European countries. They suggest that publishing in multiple languages could broaden the audience and foster diverse research perspectives, support bibliodiversity, and challenge the dominance of English. To this end, the authors propose the concept of balanced multilingualism, a dynamic approach that encompasses all communication purposes across various research fields and languages, without prioritizing any language. This approach involves creating instruments for documenting and measuring language use in research, which can facilitate a more responsible globalization of research practices. The authors conclude that while English serves as a lingua franca, it should not be the sole linguistic option. They advocate for a combination of balanced multilingualism and bibliodiversity as a more fruitful approach in cultural, identity-related, and economic terms.
'''Barnes, Lucy, and Rupert Gatti. 2019. “Bibliodiversity in Practice: Developing Community-Owned, Open Infrastructures to Unleash Open Access Publishing.” In ''ELPUB 2019 23rd Edition of the International Conference on Electronic Publishing''. Marseille, France. https://doi.org/10.4000/proceedings.elpub.2019.21.'''
:Barnes and Gatti explore the appropriateness of open access within the monograph publication ecosystem. Drawing on Geoffrey Crossick’s scholarship on open access monograph publishing, they argue that an environment for open access books requires a variety of business models. Many scholars have written about the variety of production practices that have been embraced by monograph publishers, especially those committed to open access. Where previous scholars have voiced concern about the scalability of these practices and models, Barnes and Gatti argue that scalability should not be the goal. Instead, diversity within the monograph publishing industry should be viewed as an inherent strength and that infrastructures should be developed to support “scale small.” To create such an infrastructure, agents across all sectors of the scholarly community need to work collaboratively, develop systems that mitigate the threat of a single entity capturing control of the industry, and create revenue streams that are collectively managed to support open access publishing.
'''Beigel, Fernanda, and Breno Bringel. 2023. “Circulación situada e idiomas de publicación de las élites académicas del Cono Sur.” ''Tempo Social'' 34 (January): 153–80. https://doi.org/10.11606/0103-2070.ts.2022.194375.'''
:Beigel and Bringel explore the hypercentrality of English as an academic language and its consequences, such as the loss of bibliodiversity and interculturality. They argue that this centrality reinforces inequalities, as it limits access to resources and publication opportunities for non-hegemonic countries. In this quantitative study, the authors examine researchers' self-perceptions in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile regarding publishing in English, showing that over 80% of the participants value English highly, especially in Brazil. However, differences emerge between fields: in the social sciences and humanities, over a third of academics have not published in English, while in the sciences, over 90% have. The authors propose the concept of "situated circulation" to emphasize the localized dynamics of knowledge production and argue that academic circulation is multi-scalar, affected by digital cultures and diverse mechanisms. They critique the separation of the global from the local in academic contexts, suggesting that regional and national scales are often overlooked. The study also reveals varied approaches to publishing in English. Brazil prioritizes English for internationalization and incentives, while Chile offers rewards for publishing in both Spanish and English. Argentina, though highly internationalized, allows flexibility with its own categorization system. The study shows that most publications in Argentina and Brazil are national, with a significant number of book chapters and articles, which suggests the resilience of bibliodiversity. The authors conclude that the selection of a language for publication is complex and diverse, stressing the importance of multilingualism and the need for recognizing various international circulation patterns.
'''Beigel, Fernanda, and Osvaldo Gallardo. 2021. “Productividad, bibliodiversidad y bilingüismo en un corpus completo de producciones científicas.” ''Revista Iberoamericana de Ciencia, Tecnología y Sociedad - CTS'' 16 (46): 41–71. https://www.redalyc.org/articulo.oa?id=92468651003.'''
:Beigel and Gallardo analyze the publications of scientists from the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (CONICET) and a corpus from the management and evaluation system SIGEVA in Argentina, considering disciplinary differences and language choice in scholarly publishing. They point out that the predominance of English and the salary incentives for publishing in high-impact journals are not significantly present in the field of social sciences and humanities. Nevertheless, there has been a gradual increase in the academic community’s abandonment of local languages, affecting social engagement and knowledge production, and causing a decrease in the use of other publication mediums such as books. Regarding bibliodiversity and publication types, the authors note that most disciplines focus on journal articles primarily in English, with a decrease in book chapters or books. However, the social sciences are an exception because most of their publications are books in Spanish. The tendency of publishing in English perpetuates inequalities, as many researchers believe that publishing in this language is more effective for improving the mobility and reach of their work. According to Beigel and Gallardo, it is essential to create collaborative platforms that make each nation's scientific output accessible and promote diverse cooperation to reduce the dominance of the English language in science.
'''Berger, Monica. 2021. “Bibliodiversity at the Centre: Decolonizing Open Access.” ''Development and Change'' 52 (2): 383–404. https://doi.org/10.1111/dech.12634.'''
:Berger looks at open access from a global equity perspective. She argues that the Open Access movement has not fulfilled its promise of ameliorating knowledge (and other) inequities around the world; rather the commercialization of open access and the dominance of North American and European decision-makers in the area have created a situation where those in the Global South are further excluded from academic knowledge production. Berger suggests that for the Open Access movement to fulfill its equity promises, Global South scholars need to participate from a position of self-determination and more equal knowledge transfer.
'''Galliand, Étienne, ed. 2011. “Bibliodiversity Indicators.” ''Bibliodiversity'', no. 1 (January), 1–106. https://www.alliance-editeurs.org/IMG/pdf/Bibliodiversity_Indicators.pdf'''
:The first issue of ''Bibliodiversity: Publishing and Diversity'' focuses on defining bibliodiversity— which Galliand describes as the capacity of the publishing industry to produce diversity—and outlining several indicators that can be used to measure it. The Bibliodiversity Indicators special issue features research from both academics and book industry professionals from a variety of countries. Topics explored include how to define cultural diversity, the difference between available diversity and consumed diversity, the consolidation process in the publishing industry, indicators for diversity, case studies of cultural organizations working to promote bibliodiversity, the application of a bibliodiversity index, epistemological multiversity, and the role of the state in cultural policies.  
'''Giménez Toledo, Elea, Emanuel Kulczycki'','' Janne Pölönen, and Gunnar Sivertsen. “Bibliodiversity – What It Is and Why It Is Essential to Creating Situated Knowledge.” 2019. ''Impact of Social Sciences'' (blog). December 5, 2019. https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/impactofsocialsciences/2019/12/05/bibliodiversity-what-it-is-and-why-it-is-essential-to-creating-situated-knowledge/.'''
:Giménez Toledo'','' Kulczycki'','' Pölönen, and Sivertsen discuss the importance of bibliodiversity and the role of publishers in its preservation. They argue that smaller, national publishers develop knowledge that would not exist if all publishing were to happen only at the conglomerated international level. The authors also identify monographs and book chapters as a distinctive communication pattern which requires bibliodiversity due to its multi-paradigmatic and multilingual nature and its engagement with professional and general audiences. Giménez Toledo et al. conclude that greater diversity in open access publishing is essential for rich scientific communication.
'''Hawthorne, Susan. ''Bibliodiversity A Manifesto for Independent Publishing''. North Melbourne, Victoria: Spinifex Press, 2014.'''
:Hawthorne examines issues within the global publishing industry dominated by megacorporations and explores the potential of independent publishers to promote greater cultural diversity. Hawthorne defines bibliodiversity as a self-sustaining system of storytelling and publishing where writers and producers are analogous to beings in an ecosystem. Drawing comparisons between bibliodiversity and biodiversity, tracing historical developments in book publishing and other types of media, and sharing her personal experiences, Hawthorne argues that a publishing landscape dominated by megacorporations and superstore booksellers reproduces homogenization, neglects localized contexts, and suppresses the voices of marginalized writers. In the final two chapters, Hawthorne outlines principles of bibliodiversity and lists actions that can be taken to promote bibliodiversity in the twenty-first century. She concludes by asserting that if bibliodiversity is to be genuinely embraced then ecological principles must be transformed into socio-ecological principles: these principles must be about complex systems that are in flux and reflective of constant cultural shifts.
'''Hicks, Diana, Paul Wouters, Ludo Waltman, Sarah de Rijcke, and Ismael Rafols. 2015. “Bibliometrics: The Leiden Manifesto for Research Metrics.” ''Nature News'' 520 (7548): 429. https://doi.org/10.1038/520429a.'''
:Hicks, Wouters, Waltman, De Rijcke, and Rafols document how an increasing obsession with metrics and quantitative data in research communities has negatively affected how research is conducted as well as appraised. Citing the ''h''-index and other examples of metrics that have been uncritically and therefore problematically adopted in recent decades, they argue for a more balanced, qualitative approach to evaluation. A large portion of the manifesto is dedicated to ten recommendations or “principles.” Many of the principles call for greater attention to local research contexts—including institutional policies, linguistic diversity, and competing conceptions of excellence or value; indeed, many of their principles are formulated precisely in response to methods of assessment that have demonstrably failed to account for such particulars, nuances, and variations, perpetuating reductive evaluative processes that continue to exert an undue influence on individual researchers and research ecosystems alike. Although some of the concerns raised by the authors are most relevant to other researchers and administrators whose work intersects with the field of scientometrics, the manifesto’s recommendations are of obvious significance to researchers across disciplinary and even global contexts. Even so, Hicks, Wouters, Waltman, De Rijcke, and Rafols stress that such recommendations must themselves be regularly and rigorously updated.
'''Jussieu Call Group. 2017. “Jussieu Call for Open Science and Bibliodiversity.” https://jussieucall.org/jussieu-call/.'''
:Researchers and scientific publishing professionals working within the Open Access and Scientific Publishing task force of the Bibliothèque scientifique numérique (or the Digital Scientific Library) issued this statement calling for a diversity of approaches to open access scholarship for the benefit of bibliodiversity. The group calls for the reformation of research evaluation systems, the prioritization of business models that require no payment from authors to have their research published or readers to access research, and the allocation of research funding to researchers, not publishers.
'''Leão, Delfim. “Multilingualism in Scholarly Communication: Main Findings and Future Challenges.” Presentation at the Munin Conference, 17 November. 2021, YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vK2_ZFZJUP8.'''
:In this conference presentation, Leão presents work done by the OPERAS consortium in the area of multilingualism in scholarly communication. Leão discusses the findings from a literature review on the intersection between multilingualism and scholarly communication in the social sciences and humanities. The group at OPERAS found that using English as the lingua franca does not fully address the goals of information sharing and co-construction and that multilingualism poses important advantages when it comes to achieving these goals. The group of researchers also found that the use of English databases to assess research is limiting given that so many monographs are published in local languages. Based on these findings, the group advances a view of balanced multilingualism in scholarly communications. Leão also presents the findings of a survey of scholars, translators, and publishers, including that researchers, translators, and publishers are open to viewing the advancement of multilingualism as a way to foster interculturality and equity; a collaborative system could mitigate the time, price, and flaws of the translation process; and the exchange of information among scholars who communicate in different languages within the same field of study has the potential to enrich collaboration and the visibility of research. Leão concludes by outlining recommendations to funders, policymakers, scholars, translators, and publishers to promote multilingualism.
'''Leão, Delfim, Marina Angelaki, Andrea Bertino, Suzanne Dumouchel, and Frédéric Vidal. 2018. “OPERAS Multilingualism White Paper,” https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1324026.'''
:Leão, Angelaki, Bertino, Dumouchel, and Vidal discuss the role of English as a lingua franca, intervention areas that Open Scholarly Communication in the European Research Area (OPERAS) could potentially engage with, and the work OPERAS partners are doing to promote multilingualism. Leão et al. argue that while there are advantages to the use of a lingua franca, such as wide research sharing, it also poses a challenge to the expressive capabilities of non-native speakers. The challenges associated with a lingua franca are especially pertinent within the humanities and social sciences, where language is not only a tool for communication but also the subject of study. Humanities scholars face the struggle of seeking high levels of research circulation through communicating in English while also wanting to use their own national language to achieve greater rigor and richness within their research. Leão et al. outline three key areas OPERAS could play a role in to support researchers to publish in their own language and promote transnational scientific cooperation: (1) translations, (2) the creation of a multi-language searching tool, and (3) the promotion of national language scholarly literature. OPERAS’ support for translations would primarily be in the form of advocating for open access, which indirectly supports translation efforts by removing the need to pay licenses for the translation of the work. The creation of a multi-language searching tool would involve developing a tool where users can look up a concept in one language and be referred to the articles on the same concept in a different language. The promotion of national language scholarly literature would consist of encouraging governments and organizations to support the dissemination of research in national languages. Leão et al. continue by introducing and evaluating several of their partners’ initiatives promoting multilingualism in research. The authors argue that the promotion of multilingualism should not be imagined as an English vs. all other languages dynamic; rather, multilingualism is about languages finding ways to reach audiences in a complementary fashion.
'''Makula, Amanda Y., and Laura S. Turner. 2022. “Toward Engaged Scholarship: Knowledge Inclusivity and Collaborative Collection Development between Academic Libraries and Archives and Local Public Communities.” ''College & Research Libraries'' 83 (2): 246–277. https://doi.org/10.5860/crl.83.2.246.'''
:Makula and Turner discuss the role of academic libraries and archives in movements toward more inclusive ways of knowing and community-engaged scholarship. They investigated patterns in more inclusive, community-focused collection development by surveying and interviewing academic librarians and archivists at universities across the United States. Of the 118 survey respondents included in their analysis, 76% indicated that their academic library collects, curates, or preserves materials originating from their local public community. Makula and Turner also found that in community-oriented projects, survey respondents were twice as likely to report working with unpublished archival material as opposed to circulating or non-archival material. Libraries opening their archives to materials created and/or owned by local public communities is reflective of a broader movement within academia towards including traditionally marginalized perspectives in scholarly projects. Makula and Turner conclude that through integrating locally produced forms of knowledge into academic libraries, universities can create new learning environments for students and faculty and open the academy to those whose knowledge has been traditionally excluded from scholarly conversations.
'''Ochsner, Michael, Nina Kancewicz-Hoffman, Marek Hołowiecki, and Jon Holm. 2020. ''Overview of Peer Review Practices in the SSH.'' figshare. https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12032589.v2.'''
:Ochsner et al. edit this report that addresses the challenges that peer review poses to the humanities and social sciences, especially in Europe. Challenges to peer review in the HSS disciplines include the importance of local and national languages, the diversity of publication outputs (particularly books and monographs), a lack of clear criteria to evaluate scholarship, and conflicting research paradigms between reviewers and authors. These challenges are additional to other peer review issues across academic disciplines, such as gender and regional bias, and the increasing workload placed on reviewers. Despite these issues, the authors state that some form of peer review is required to evaluate HSS research, but it should acknowledge disciplinary particularities, the local embeddedness of research, and its societal impact.
'''“Open Insights: An Interview with Leslie Chan.” 2018. Open Library of Humanities. Accessed May 10, 2022. https://www.openlibhums.org/news/314/.'''
:In this interview, Chan discusses the movement towards the internationalization of research, the opportunities and challenges of open access, and initiatives focused on making knowledge production more equitable. He argues that the internationalization agenda often results in researchers from the Global South having to conform to the theoretical approaches from the North, abandoning locally situated research, and writing in English only. Chan asserts that the Open Access movement provides an important opportunity to rethink what is really meant by openness. Ultimately, he argues that introducing openness into an asymmetrical knowledge system amplifies the gaps within the system, especially when that openness is obtained through models that charge authors during the publication process. Chan advocates for innovative and diverse models of openness to promote justice and equality in research.
'''Ortega, Élika. 2019. “Zonas de Contacto: A Digital Humanities Ecology of Knowledges.” In ''Debates in the Digital Humanities 2019'', edited by Matthew K. Gold and Lauren F. Klein, 179–87. University of Minnesota Press. https://doi.org/10.5749/j.ctvg251hk.18.'''
:Ortega considers the field of digital humanities and its concentration of English-language work and output. She argues that the purposeful facilitation of zones of contact between practitioners from different regions who work in different languages would support a more diverse ecology of knowledges for the field. Ortega examines the efforts made by groups like the Alliance of Digital Humanities Organisations to encourage multilingual engagement but concludes that these efforts have not, so far, been successful in diversifying the output and interaction of the field in a major way. For Ortega, this work is critical for the ongoing sustenance and evolution of digital humanities as a field and community.
'''Rio Riande, Gimena del 2022. “¿En qué lengua citamos cuando escribimos sobre Humanidades Digitales?” ''Revista de Humanidades Digitales'' 7:127–43. https://www.aacademica.org/gimena.delrio.riande/189.'''
:Del Rio Riande examines 9,850 references from 510 articles published on Hispanic digital humanities journals to explore the languages included in their references. The author argues that the inequalities in the circulation of knowledge in digital humanities, especially in Hispanic America, are greater because academia is built on an unequal and segmented structure of knowledge production and circulation with a mainstream circuit and other peripheral ones. Consequently, Hispanic researchers in this field are often not represented in mainstream indexes or databases, and there is a clear tendency to cite Anglophone scholars. This means that although writing is done in Spanish, citations in this language are slight. This is reflected in the fact that in the articles written in Spanish, 47.55% of the references are in Spanish and 47.49% are in English, whereas Anglophone articles only have 11.47% references in Spanish. These results confirm the presence of Anglophone monolingualism in digital humanities publications both for writing and citing. Del Rio Riande concludes that most Anglophone academics hardly cite resources in languages other than English due to the value given to mainstream Anglophone journals of the Global North. Thus, many researchers end up writing in English and citing Anglophone sources, although there is a greater diversity of languages when citing secondary sources. Despite these inequalities, Del Rio Riande emphasizes that the goal is not to replace one language with another but to implement the concept of balanced multilingualism, which implies that communicating in a lingua franca does not necessarily mean adopting a single language.
'''Rovelli, Laura. 2021. “Herramienta 2: Para promover la bibliodiversidad y defender el multilingüismo.” CLACSO (blog). November 10, 2021. https://www.clacso.org/herramienta-2-para-promover-la-bibliodiversidad-y-defender-el-multilinguismo/.'''
:Rovelli emphasizes the potential of Latin America and the Caribbean to promote diverse knowledge dissemination in various formats and languages while balancing global standards with local needs. This would involve creating new bibliodiverse evaluation indicators to complement traditional metrics, which typically reflect the production of scholarship in English published in mainstream journals. The author points out that in scholarly publishing and open science, significant concerns include international inequalities in digital infrastructure, increasing commercialization, and the dominance of English for interoperability. To address these issues, Latin America has established documentation centers to standardize bibliographic norms and enhance research circulation, followed by the creation of regional libraries and open access repositories. Despite the recency of these efforts and the reliance on English-dominated databases such as Scopus or Web of Science, the region boasts four indexing multilingual repositories: Latindex, SciELO, Readlyc, and Biblat. In the social sciences and humanities, book production remains crucial for in-depth research, even as concerns around intellectual property in the digital age persist due to its impact on how knowledge is disseminated and controlled. University presses are increasingly important in supporting open access and bibliodiversity, as well as for countering commercialization trends. Rovelli advocates for evaluation systems that support multilingualism and encourage scholarly production not just in Spanish and Portuguese but also in Indigenous languages. This aligns with the goal of bibliodiversity of valuing diverse formats, languages, and knowledge distribution channels, and prioritizing the global scholarly dialogue over the commercial interests of publishing oligopolies.
'''Schalkwyk, François van, and Thierry M Luescher. 2017. “The African University Press.” Cape Town, South Africa: African Minds. https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/144850511.pdf.'''
:This report examines the African university press landscape, showing a small but active group of university presses and the opportunities and constraints they face. The report revealed that only 15 out of 52 university presses have published titles from 2012 to 2015 (the most recent years at the date of publication), which implies that most of their publications are not discoverable online, and many presses have not adapted to technological advances or invested in open access. The study highlights that higher education publishing has become a competitive business focused on market position and share value. However, there is potential for a new economic model called social capitalism, which is based on collaboration and sharing. African university presses have the opportunity to enhance their international presence by adopting digital and technological innovations but must adapt their workflows and marketing strategies. The authors conclude that future discussions about the university press in Africa should focus less on funding and more on reinventing how the press can operate and thrive with the new possibilities afforded by digitization and the internet. Some of the recommendations based on the findings are creating a network of university presses across Africa to share resources and stimulate innovation, emphasizing the value of university presses in the publishing process of academic monographs, and unlocking funding for open access.
'''Shearer, Kathleen, and Arianna Becerril-García. 2021. “Decolonizing Scholarly Communications through Bibliodiversity.” Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4423997.'''
:Shearer and Becerril-García argue that the consolidation of the publishing industry and reliance on journal-based citation measures to evaluate researchers has negatively impacted bibliodiversity and colonized scholarly communications. They assert that, if we are to achieve greater equity within systems of knowledge production, then bibliodiversity is central. The informal, localized, and non-commercial nature of scholarly communication infrastructure in Latin America makes it a prime example of a system that supports bibliodiversity. More traditional models of open access scholarship also provide opportunities for fostering bibliodiversity, but the popular “pay to publish” model risks excluding knowledge emerging from the Global South. Shearer and Becerril-García conclude that fostering greater bibliodiversity within scholarly communications requires (1) the development of new, sustainable funding for a range of publications and (2) the adoption of assessment measures that incentivize researchers to publish in a range of publications. By its nature, bibliodiversity requires respecting difference and connecting diversity across research services, outputs, and perspectives.
'''Shearer, Kathleen, Leslie Chan, Iryna Kuchma, and Pierre Mounier. 2020. “Fostering Bibliodiversity in Scholarly Communications: A Call for Action!” ''Copyright, Fair Use, Scholarly Communication, Etc.'', April. https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/scholcom/152.'''
:Shearer, Chan, Kuchma, and Mounier argue that fostering bibliodiversity is critical for a healthy ecosystem of knowledge. Building on the principles of the Jussieu Call to Action, they identify several challenges to bibliodiversity and strategies for addressing them. The dominance of the English language across scientific publishing has resulted in research that is not reflective of intercultural practices, which inhibits societies from taking advantage of research done where they live. A strong scholarly communication system must balance the benefits of English as a lingua franca while also preserving the value of research in a variety of languages. The consolidation of publishers in the academic sector has the potential to lock research communities into particular services and minimizes their role in the development of services. In order for bibliodiversity to flourish, there needs to be diverse, open, and community-driven research infrastructures which function alongside a common set of open principles. The limited funding models for libraries makes fewer resources available for supporting smaller and more diverse research services and infrastructure. Alternative funding schemes need to be adopted to support a diversity of research services and infrastructures. Current research evaluation methods, which emphasize the prestige of academic journals and citation counts, stunt bibliodiversity. To foster a healthy knowledge ecosystem, research needs to be evaluated through expert judgment and more qualitative criteria. Promoting bibliodiversity within the current context requires the intentional and coordinated efforts between funders, libraries, policy makers, and researchers.
'''Shiva, Vandana. 1993. “Monocultures of the Mind—Understanding the Threats to Biological and Cultural Diversity.” ''Indian Journal of Public Administration'' 39 (3): 237–48. https://doi.org/10.1177/0019556119930304.'''
:Shiva discusses biological, economic, political, and knowledge-based monocultures. As an analogy to agricultural monocultures, monocultures of the mind inhibit our ability to see through the lens of diversity, excludes a range of possibilities while simultaneously making us ignorant to these exclusions. The dissonance between monocultures of the mind and the world’s biological, cultural, epistemic, economic, and political diversity means that monoculture creates “apartheid”: difference is perceived as inferiority, leading to inequality. These dynamics of monoculture are reflected in political systems, economic systems, and legal frameworks. Examples include the reduction of Third World democratic movements to “tribalism” and the domination of western market economies over sustenance economies. In order to protect the knowledge emanating from Third World communities, monocultures and bioimperialism (the idea that only knowledge from western corporations needs protection) must be challenged.
'''Siversten, Gunnar. 2018. “Balanced Multilingualism in Science.” ''BiD: Textos Universitaris de Biblioteconomia i Documentació'', no. 40. https://doi.org/10.1344/BiD2018.40.25.'''
:Siversten demonstrates how the significance of language in scientific practice and communication has become invisible on a global scale, as reflected in research policy published and discussed in English. While having a common language for the knowledge market is useful, the function of language is frequently overlooked. The author proposes the notion of balanced multilingualism, which entails considering all communication goals in diverse research areas, as well as the languages required to accomplish these purposes, holistically, and without exclusions or priority. This concept also advocates for the development of mechanisms to document and measure the use of language for various research goals, providing the basis for monitoring the increasing globalization of research in a more responsible path. The goal of balanced multilingualism is to eliminate the existing dichotomy between English and other languages, replacing the current hierarchy with a useful concept for understanding and promoting both scientific globalization and societally responsible research.  Due to the prevalence or dominance of English in science, a new balance should be struck so other languages can still be used in settings where they serve a more efficient function. Siversten mentions the social sciences and humanities as an example, as they combine international excellence with local relevance in a multilingual setting. The author concludes that balanced multilingualism emerges as a powerful and strategic response to the tensions between international scientific collaboration, research excellence, and societal impact. It champions the recognition and use of diverse languages in scientific communication, ensuring that research not only achieves global reach but also fosters deep engagement with local contexts and societal needs. By advocating for equitable language policies and inclusive evaluation criteria, balanced multilingualism aligns with the principles of open science.
'''Snijder, Ronald. 2022. “Big in Japan, Zimbabwe or Brazil – Global Reach and National Preferences for Open Access Books.” ''Insights'' 35. https://doi.org/10.1629/uksg.580.'''
:Snijder examines the perceived effect of internationalization on publishing, which places a greater emphasis on global issues, typically written in English only. This raises the question of whether global interest leads to a shift away from regional concerns. To explore this, he conducted a systemic analysis of global readers’ preferences by examining the usage of the OAPEN library’s open access collection. The study is based on the most downloaded social sciences and humanities books in 100 countries over a 12-month period. The author highlights that in academic writing, there is an evident tension between English as a lingua franca enabling global research against local languages that provide a better cultural fit, so multilingualism can be viewed through the lens of center and periphery dynamics. The findings show that readers increasingly favored books in their local languages over English. This is evident in Mexico and Latin America, where Spanish is predominant (except for Brazil), whereas Europe has a more diverse choice of languages. While these results might seem contrary to the idea of English as the lingua franca of research, Snijder argues that they point toward a global interest in regionally focused literature. When given access to a freely available collection, most readers choose books that cover topics relevant to their country, deviating from English-language monographs. This challenges the notion of absolute English dominance in scholarly communication and highlights the significance of bibliodiversity.
'''“Who Gets Published?” n.d. How Books Are Made. Accessed June 28, 2024. https://howbooksaremade.com/episodes/who-gets-published/.'''
:In this podcast, Arthur Attwell and Anasuya Sengupta discuss where book publishing fits into the universe of human knowledge, and what visions and ideas constitute it. They assert that the most important decision in publishing is who gets published. This question is deeply embedded within the framework of decolonization, as it involves addressing the intersectionality of power dynamics that influence which voices and perspectives are prioritized or marginalized in the dissemination of knowledge. The podcast also explores how people’s lived experience is frequently overlooked in the books that are published. This is because most books are written in a restricted number of languages, and market forces, biases, and editorial trends influence language selection. Atwell and Sengupta argue that diversity in publishing is important because it allows for more perspectives to be represented, but they also recognize that books are not the only way to share knowledge and that other formats, such as audio, can increase the availability and accessibility of diverse bodies of literature. ==Initiatives and Organizations==
