'''“African Books Collective: About Us.” n.d. Accessed July 10, 2024. https://www.africanbookscollective.com/about-us.'''
:African Books Collective (ABC) is a worldwide marketing and distribution outlet for books from Africa. It mainly distributes scholarly and academic books, literature, general culture, and children's books. Books written in any language are accepted, especially those in African languages. ABC represents independent publishers, including university presses, research institutes, NGOs, and commercial publishers, both large and small. It seeks to be profit-making on behalf of its publishers and non-profit on its own behalf. ABC has a section dedicated to books, another to eBooks and catalogs, and the website readafricanbooks.com, which profiles the work of African publishers and authors.
'''“AfricArXiv.” n.d. AfricArXiv. Accessed May 22, 2024. https://africarxiv.pubpub.org/.'''
:AfricArXiv is a free, community-led digital repository dedicated to African research, with the goal of creating an independent and open repository for scholars across the continent. This initiative fosters collaboration among African researchers and facilitates knowledge exchange with their non-African counterparts, ensuring that African scholarship reaches a global audience. Additionally, AfricArXiv collaborates on several initiatives to preserve and share knowledge across a range of disciplines, with an emphasis on using a variety of African languages in research and technology. Some of these initiatives include LANFRICA, a language-focused search engine that allows the search for information related to African languages, and the African Digital Rights Network, which is formed by analysts, activists, and academics with the goal of conducting research on digital rights in Africa. The platform serves as a credible, reliable and multidisciplinary repository that makes text, data, and information easily searchable and accessible online.
'''“AmeliCA Open Science - AmeliCA.” n.d. Accessed May 21, 2024. http://amelica.org/.'''
:AmeliCA Open Science is a non-profit collaborative initiative of scholarly nature that released in 2018 in Latin America, supported by UNESCO, CLACSO, and Redalyc. They also include other parts of the Global South, such as Asia and Africa, in their mission to support the development of diverse open science projects. With an emphasis on diversity, multilingualism, universal rights, and equity, AmeliCA seeks to improve the uptake of open science based on the paradigm of the commons.
'''“Cultivate Your Knowledge- Érudit”. Accessed July 11, 2024. https://www.erudit.org/en/.'''
:Érudit ensures the digital dissemination of scientific and cultural publications within the humanities and social sciences. It serves as a significant Canadian and global platform for dissemination, while also functioning as a distinctive technological and service infrastructure designed to establish an innovative model that enhances access to knowledge and supports bibliodiversity. Moreover, Érudit offers services such as data tagging, documentation indexing for international content aggregators, and access to comprehensive corpora for users. By advocating for open access and employing diverse dissemination strategies, Érudit promotes research and facilitates universal access to knowledge, transcending geographical and financial barriers.
'''“Directory of Open Access Journals – DOAJ.” 2024. May 3, 2024. https://doaj.org/.'''
:The Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) is a non-profit organization that serves as an international index for a variety of open access publications. It is a global community comprised of volunteers, team members, ambassadors, and partnerships from various nations. Its goal is to build a diverse, equitable ecosystem where credible research can be accessed freely online, regardless of discipline, geography, or language. DOAJ’s review application process is assisted by volunteers and partners. It promotes open access and excellent practices in different locations through ambassadors. Furthermore, through collaborations with organizations, DOAJ can trade information, services, and access to information resources that help index journals.
'''DORA Group. 2012. “San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment.” Accessed July 20, 2021. https://sfdora.org/read/.'''
:The San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA) offers recommendations for improving how the quality of research outputs is assessed, focusing on peer-reviewed journal articles but acknowledging the importance of datasets and other types of outputs. It was developed at the 2016 Annual Meeting of The American Society for Cell Biology (ASCB) in San Francisco, in large part as a response to concerns about the journal impact factor (JIF) being used as a proxy metric for scholarly merit. It offers recommendations for funding agencies, institutions, researchers, publishers, researchers, and organizations that supply metrics as well as a general recommendation against using journal-level metrics such as the journal impact factor to assess individual articles.
'''Federation of Finnish Learned Societies, The Committee for Public Information, The Finnish Association for Scholarly Publishing, Universities Norway, and European Network for Research Evaluation in the Social Sciences and the Humanities. 2019. “Helsinki Initiative on Multilingualism in Scholarly Communication,” April. https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.7887059.v1.'''
:The Helsinki Initiative calls for greater protection of multilingualism within academic publishing to maximize the impact of research. Specifically, it calls for (1) supporting research dissemination for the benefit of society, (2) protecting infrastructures for publishing locally relevant research, and (3) promoting language diversity in research assessment and funding.
'''“Geopolitics of Academic Production.” 2017. ''The Knowledge G.A.P.'' (blog). August 24, 2017. http://knowledgegap.org/.'''
:The Knowledge Geopolitics of Academic Production or the Knowledge G.A.P. is a research group focused on “understanding whether there is an unequal and underrepresentation of academic content produced in and by ‘Global South’ researchers and […] the various mechanisms and power dimensions through which such structures of inequality and exclusion are actively produced, reproduced, and embedded in the global publishing system.” The group also seeks to “examine the implications of such inequalities in regard to diversity of knowledge, cognitive justice, equitable collaboration, and sustainable development at large.”
'''“International Alliance of Independent Publishers.” n.d. Accessed July 11, 2024. https://www.alliance-editeurs.org/?lang=en.'''
:The International Alliance of Independent Publishers is a professional collective that unites over 800 independent publishers from more than 60 countries. It is organized into six language networks (English, Arabic, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Persian) as well as thematic groups. The alliance aims to promote and foster bibliodiversity. To this end, the Bibliodiversity Observatory was established to evaluate and enhance bibliodiversity across various regions of the world and to organize international professional meetings and thematic workshops to facilitate collaboration among independent publishers. Moreover, it supports international editorial projects to increase text circulation and promote equitable access for readers. The alliance also encourages affinity groups among catalogs, online project fairs, and assists in organizing sessions and co-editions.
'''“LA Referencia - Inicio.” n.d. Accessed July 10, 2024. https://www.lareferencia.info/es/.'''
:LA Referencia is a network of repositories that, through its services, supports national open access strategies and the visibility of scientific production in Latin America and Spain. Its objective is to promote open access to scientific production in Latin America as a public good, and to achieve economies of scale by agreeing on common interoperable guidelines, transferable open-source technologies, among others. Additionally, it seeks to establish alliances with international actors and organizations. The platform implements national nodes of the countries that make up LA Referencia to integrate scientific articles, doctoral and master’s theses from universities and institutions from these countries.
'''“OCSDNET | Catalysing Open and Collaborative Science for Development Opportunities in the Global South.” n.d. Accessed July 18, 2022. http://ocsdnet.org/.'''
:Bringing together 12 researcher–practitioner teams from the Global South, the Open and Collaborative Science in Development Network (OCSDNet) investigates how open, collaborative approaches to science could help in the achievement of development goals. Its work includes supporting research projects, building community, identifying barriers, and furthering Open and Collaborative Science in Development as an area of study.
'''“OPERAS.” n.d. OPERAS. Accessed July 18, 2022. https://www.operas-eu.org/.'''
:OPERAS (Open Scholarly Communication in the European Research Area for Social Sciences and Humanities) works to advance open science in Europe in the social sciences and humanities by coordinating and federating infrastructure resources. Its special interest groups work collaboratively on projects related to a specific topic. The Special Interest Group on Multilingualism supports multilingualism in research publications, including by developing translation services and a multilingual discovery tool.
'''“Public Knowledge Project.” n.d. Public Knowledge Project. Accessed July 11, 2024. https://pkp.sfu.ca/.'''
:The Public Knowledge Project (PKP) is an academic initiative that promotes knowledge democratization and open access. It employs open-source publishing platforms to support the dissemination of journals and books in open access. Additionally, it develops and continues to improve free and open-source software (FOSS) publishing platforms and workflows, namely Open Journal Systems (OJS), Open Monograph Press (OMP), and Open Preprint Systems (OPS). This software is licensed to be freely shared, installed, and modified, which has contributed to cooperation and collaboration for the continuous growth of open science. Thousands of journals use these publishing platforms, especially in South-eastern Asia, Latin America, and Eastern Europe. Originating as a research endeavor to enhance access to scholarly publications, PKP has evolved by integrating principles of open science, related economic and legal models, metadata, social media, and historical insights into their software. This evolution has led to the development of innovative tools and the promotion of open infrastructures aimed at facilitating access to open science.
'''“SciELO.Org.” n.d. Accessed July 11, 2024. https://scielo.org/es/.'''
:SciELO is an international platform promoting scholarly communication through open access. It operates in a decentralized manner to support this public policy globally. SciELO manages collections of research communication objects, including articles and various document types, and aligns national journals with current scientific editing standards. By implementing the Diamond open access model and CC-BY licenses, SciELO enhances accessibility to scientific literature, positioning participating countries as leaders in open access. Its goals include fostering international scientific cooperation, promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion, and ensuring high scientific quality. SciELO facilitates open science by providing infrastructure for the complete research cycle, using virtual platforms to maximize research visibility and impact. {{Navigation|previous=Epistemic Injustice|next=Indigenous Knowledges}} {{BookCat}}

Engaging Knowledge Diversity/Community K.text:
==Definitions== '''Community-based research''' '''(CBR)''': Research designed and conducted through collaboration between researchers and community members that takes place in community settings. CBR is a complex term that is often used interchangeably with terms such as “activist anthropology,” “collaborative community-based research,” “collaborative research,” “community-based participatory research,” “engaged scholarship,” “participatory action research,” “practitioner inquiry,” “public sociology,” and “translational research.” '''Action Research''': A type of research methodology in which research is conducted about an object of study and is at the same time applied toward changing the object of study, which is often a social phenomenon or system. ==Resources==
'''Bandy, J., Mary F. Price, P. H. Clayton, J. Metzker, G. Nigro, S. Stanlick, S. Etheridge Woodson, A. Bartel, and S. Gale. 2018. “Democratically Engaged Assessment: Reimagining the Purposes and Practices of Assessment in Community Engagement.” https://hdl.handle.net/1805/17729.'''
:Bandy et al. propose a conceptual framework and practical guidance for the assessment of community engagement, considering its civic potential by performing democratically engaged assessment (DEA). This approach focuses on being and doing with the community, co-creating knowledge through multi-directional flows of ideas, transformative collaborations, and following values of co-creation, rigor, full participation, generativity, practicability, and resilience. To achieve this, practical guidance is offered to include DEA in the typical phases of assessment and among multiple stakeholders, such as communities, higher education institutions, students, and faculty. The authors conclude that assessment practices can challenge the normative paradigms that often limit the transformative potential of community engagement, but it requires developing critical and holistic methods that follow democratic values.
'''Banks, Sarah, Andrea Armstrong, Anne Bonner, Yvonne Hall, Patrick Harman, Luke Johnston, Clare Levi, Kath Smith and Ruth Taylor. “Between Research and Community Development: Negotiating a Contested Space for Collaboration and Creativity.” In ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 21–48. Bristol University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.8.'''
:Banks et al. discuss challenges and opportunities of co-produced research projects and address debates around whether forms of co-produced research and community development are distinguishable. Scholars argue that co-produced research, specifically participatory-action research (PAR), confuses community development with research. Banks et al. concede that given the continuous cycle from reflection to research to action, it is essentially impossible to reach a point where it can be said that something is research or community development. However, what arguably sets PAR apart from community development is that those engaging in PAR explicitly intend to study something. Banks et al. explore the dynamics of co-produced research through outlining the work done within ''Imagine North East'': a co-produced research project in North East England which investigated past, present, and future community development projects. Through exploring the three different components of ''Imagine North East'', Banks et al. found that the co-inquiry process enabled partners to see the bigger historical, regional, and international picture of which they are a part. Banks et al. also identified key lessons: that it takes time to develop a shared aim, purpose, vision, and degree of trust within co-inquiry groups but that these attributes are vital to success.
'''Banks, Sarah, Andrea Armstrong, Mark Booth, Greg Brown, Kathleen Carter, Maurice Clarkson, Lynne Corner, et al. 2014. “Using Co-Inquiry to Study Co-Inquiry: Community-University Perspectives on Research.” ''Journal of Community Engagement and Scholarship'' 7 (1): 37–47. https://doi.org/10.54656/GRXT3521.'''
:Banks et al. explore co-inquiry as a research process through co-inquiry: a group of community partners, academics, and researchers collaborated to explore trends and patterns across four different case studies of co-inquiry projects. The group’s work was modelled after the concept of cooperative experiential inquiry and drew on the methodologies of community development work, critical community practice, and critical pedagogy. Through dialogue between community members and academics, the group identified several themes. Community members raised the issue of academic jargon repeatedly. Banks et al. argue that the issue of academic language is about more than just terminology: it has to do with power differentials, academic culture, and ways of knowing. For academics, the complications of occupying more than one role in a research project were challenging. Additionally, the group identified six benefits of engaging in co-inquiry action research which include: (1) broadening of theoretical knowledge, (2) developing practical knowledge, (3) deepening sensitivity, (4) stimulating reflexivity, (5) developing self-confidence, and (6) leading to further action. Ultimately, the group was able to address these challenges and create a space of collaborative reflexivity where co-inquirers were able to reflect on themselves, the influence of their position on the group, and importantly, the structure and dynamics of the group itself. Banks et al. conclude by advocating for the integration of co-inquiry action research groups within larger research projects rather than simply as advisory groups.
'''Banks, Sarah, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl and Paul Ward. ''“''Co-producing Research: A Community Development Approach''.”'' In ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 1–18. Bristol University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.7.'''
:In the introductory chapter of ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', Banks et al. contextualize the ''Imagine - Connecting Communities through Research'' project and explain what is meant by a community development approach to the co-production of research. The ''Imagine'' project brought together academics, artists, museum educators, youth workers, community workers, activists, local residents, teachers, young people, and policymakers to investigate the historical and social dynamics of civic engagement. It serves as the primary example used throughout the book to explore themes related to the co-production of research. Banks et al. outline the major points of contention when defining co-production of research and community development which include what is truly meant by “community” and differences between co-produced research and community development practice. The authors define a community development approach to co-production as several partners with diverse perspectives engaging collaboratively in research that develops communities, builds the capacity for action, and works for social change.
'''Bell, David, Steve Pool, Kim Streets and Natalie Walton, with Kate Pahl. ''“''How Does Arts Practice Inform a Community Development Approach to the Co-production of Research?''.”'' In ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 95–114. Bristol University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.11.'''
:This chapter presents a dialogue between the authors: a researcher (David Bell), an artist (Steve Pool), a chief executive of a museum service (Kim Streets), and an arts educator (Natalie Walton) about how arts can be leveraged to imagine better futures and methods and trends within collaborative research. The first part of the dialogue focuses on the ways arts projects can and cannot empower communities to imagine better futures, with an emphasis on how class influences practices of re-imagining. The second part of the dialogue explores the historical, political, and economic dimensions of community-university partnerships. Central to this conversation is an interrogation of language and terminology. David Bell argues that the word “community” can often serve as a “dog whistle term,” invoking only certain kinds of communities. The chapter concludes by outlining several lessons gathered from the conversation: arts can be used to explore—and reproduce—social tensions, hierarchies, and contradiction; it is at the in-betweenness of conversations that collective knowledge can emerge; and building a more equitable society requires the forces of art, culture, and research, although these forces often get restricted. '' ''
'''Cameron, Josh, Beverly Wenger-Trayner, Etienne Wenger-Trayner, Angie Hart, Lisa Buttery, Elias Kourkoutas, Suna Eryigit-Madzwamuse and Anne Rathbone. ''“''Community-University Partnership Research Retreats: A Productive Force for Developing Communities of Research Practice''.”'' In ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 69–92. Bristol University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.10.'''
:Cameron et al. discuss the dynamics of using a community of practice (CoP) framework as an analytical tool and an approach to collaborative research projects. Central to this exploration is that boundaries that exist within these collaborations, whether cultural boundaries or boundaries between academic and non-academic partners, are opportunities to deepen collective learning. Cameron et al. argue that key to the ''Imagine'' project’s CoP, which involved a variety of partners focused on the theme of resilience, was that the group’s goal was to positively leverage boundary tensions rather than eliminate them. The authors outline several key challenges for the CoP, which included differences across sources of knowledge, power differentials within knowledge production contexts, uncertainties around what the CoP’s outcomes could be, and differences in worldviews. The evolution of the group is then tracked through the stages of Wenger et al.’s maturity model: potential, coalescing, maturing, stewardship, and transformation. Cameron et al. conclude by exploring the critical practices that enabled the CoP to sustain their work over five years and create enduring transformations, which include implementing multiple modes of interaction, drawing the research partners into each other’s worlds, disrupting comfort zones, establishing spaces for reflexivity and acknowledgment of emotions, holding research retreats in non-academic or neutral spaces, employing a variety of recording techniques, distributing leadership, and the presence of boundary spanners who occupy different positions within the CoP.
'''Glass, Ronald David, and Anne Newman. 2015. “Ethical and Epistemic Dilemmas in Knowledge Production: Addressing Their Intersection in Collaborative, Community-Based Research.” ''Theory and Research in Education'' 13 (1): 23–37. https://doi.org/10.1177/1477878515571178.'''
:Glass and Newman discuss the opportunities for collaborative community-based research (CCBR) to address the epistemic injustices embedded within knowledge production. They argue that Miranda Fricker’s emphasis on addressing epistemic injustice through individual virtue misses out on structural remedies and that Elizabeth Anderson’s institutional solutions are not robust enough. CCBR, while not an absolute remedy to injustices present in knowledge production, does provide a robust response to epistemic injustice by centring ethical-epistemic dynamics within its methodology. Through embedding epistemic agency for communities in knowledge production and positioning itself at the intersection of expert and non-specialists’ knowledge, CCBR is a powerful tool for addressing the testimonial and hermeneutical injustice that emerges when so-called lay knowledge is denigrated as illegitimate. Glass and Newman call for universities to offer greater support for CCBR but encourage caution given that universities have histories of posing threats to a variety of communities.
'''Heron, John, and Peter Reason. 1997. “A Participatory Inquiry Paradigm.” ''Qualitative Inquiry'' 3 (3): 274–94. https://doi.org/10.1177/107780049700300302.'''
:Heron and Reason offer a philosophical and theoretical critique of Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba’s paradigms of research which include positivism, postpositivism, critical theory, and constructivism. They argue that the model fails to account for the participatory worldview, which relies on subjective-objective reality where knowing is at the interface between the subject and what the subject encounters. The authors theorize that a participative worldview also involves an extended epistemology which includes four interrelated ways of knowing: experiential, presentational, propositional, and practical. A methodology based on a participative worldview, which Heron and Reason refer to as cooperative inquiry, is fully collaborative, balances action and reflection, and recognizes that researchers are also subjects and subjects are also researchers. This methodology rests on two principles: epistemic participation and political participation. Heron and Reason also argue that Lincoln and Guba’s outline of paradigms fails to address the axiological question: What sort of knowledge is intrinsically valuable in human life? According to a participative worldview, practical knowledge is intrinsically valuable. They assert that a participative worldview is a more satisfying and appropriate paradigm or “myth” for our time than the current western worldview.
'''Loggins, John, Christopher Nayve, and Star Plaxton-Moore. 2020. ''How to Facilitate an Exploration of Epistemic Justice & Community Engagement Through Stories''. Campus Compact, YouTube, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zWIt_pKuQYs.'''
:Loggins, Nayve, and Plaxton-Moore argue that the academy has systematically excluded and denigrated community-based knowledge, thus contributing to epistemic injustice. Community engagement, on the other hand, is focused on creating space for community-situated knowledge and wisdom. Weaving together their own personal experiences with the intersections between epistemic (in)justice and community engagement, Loggins, Nayve, and Plaxton-Moore argue that genuine epistemic justice cannot occur when community wisdom is perceived as an “add-on.” For justice to occur, community-based knowledge must be embedded into the academy. Making space for community wisdom requires both small-scale action (self-reflection, deep listening, naming unjust dynamics within groups) and structural action (challenging concepts of authority, shifting locations of knowledge production).
'''London, Rebecca A., Ronald David Glass, Ethan Chang, Sheeva Sabati, and Saugher Nojan. 2022. “‘We Are About Life Changing Research’: Community Partner Perspectives on Community-Engaged Research Collaborations.” ''Journal of Higher Education Outreach and Engagement'' 26 (1). https://openjournals.libs.uga.edu/jheoe/article/view/2512.'''
:London, Glass, Chang, Sabati, and Nojan explore the ethical, political, and material dimensions of knowledge production within community-engaged research, focusing on communities’ motivations and experiences. Through in-depth interviews with 15 community partners who received funding from the Center for Collaborative Research for an Equitable California, they identified several themes relating to the process of knowledge production. Community members often enter research partnerships because they want to translate what they know anecdotally into something “solid,” and to materially improve the lives of their communities. London et al. discuss the “double bind of legitimacy” faced by community partners: knowledge of community members is often deemed as unsophisticated and subjective, and university partnerships lend community knowledge legitimacy. However, depending on academic legitimacy undermines the community’s epistemic authority and can indirectly perpetuate their experiences with epistemic injustice. Community partners also found the time-intensive realities of academic publishing in direct tension with their pressing advocacy goals. London et al. argue that to address the compounding realities of material and epistemic injustice, those engaged in community partnerships must (1) understand that research is not inherently good and can perpetuate multiple forms of epistemic injustice; (2) attend to the complicated connections between ethics, politics, and the production of knowledge; and (3) be responsive to the short-term and long-term needs of community partners.
'''Martikke, Susanne, Andrew Church and Angie Hart. ''“''A Radical Take on Co-Production? Community Partner Leadership in Research''.”'' In ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 49–68. Bristol University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.9.'''
:Martikke, Church, and Hart discuss their process researching co-inquiry projects as a community-university partnership (CUP) and several key implications for the field of research co-production. The CUP consisted of one community-based researcher (Martikke) and two academic researchers (Church and Hart). Through reflecting on their own experiences within a CUP and data gathered through interviewing researchers engaged in research co-production, the authors identified key lessons. CUPs are inherently unpredictable, and partners will likely have different expectations within the research process; acknowledging this unpredictability, seeing differences in expectations as part of the learning process, and working through subsequent challenges are necessary and strengthen partnerships in the long run. Research that emerges from CUPs is often better and different than research done solely by academics; however, CUP work is more time intensive. Those engaged in CUPs should be aware that many of the benefits of this kind of research are afforded to those individuals and organizations directly involved and that benefits to wider communities usually take longer to materialize. Martikke, Church, and Hart conclude that the sustainability of CUPs depends largely on individual leadership and commitment to these partnerships.
'''McAteer, Mary, and Lesley Wood. 2018. “Decolonising Knowledge: Enacting the Civic Role of the University in a Community-Based Project.” ''South African Journal of Education'' 38 (4). https://doi.org/10.4314/saje.v38i4.'''
:McAteer and Wood discuss the civic role of the university and democratization of knowledge production in context to a participatory action research (PAR) project in South Africa where academic researchers, local primary teachers, and teaching assistants collaborated to create a manual for students’ parents. McAteer and Wood introduce two models of the civic role of the university. One model emphasizes the university as the well-intentioned giver of knowledge and the other model emphasizes the university as a co-constructor of knowledge. McAteer and Wood argue that by seeking to enact the latter model in their PAR project, the academics and teaching assistants were able to co-produce knowledge and develop epistemic democracy. Through approaching the research with a facilitative model rather than a teaching model, the academic researchers were able to shift the structural dimension of the relationships that existed within the partnership largely impacted by the historical legacy of apartheid. McAteer and Wood conclude by calling attention to the ways that the institutional contexts of universities need to be transformed in order for the decolonization and democratization of knowledge to occur through engaged scholarship.
'''Paphitis, Sharli Anne. 2018. “The Possibility of Addressing Epistemic Injustice through Engaged Research Practice: Reflections on a Menstruation Related Critical Health Education Project in South Africa.” ''Critical Public Health'' 28 (3): 363–72. https://doi.org/10.1080/09581596.2017.1418500.'''
:Paphitis discusses the potential for community-engaged research to mitigate epistemic injustice through drawing on two experiences with menstruation related projects in South Africa. In the first case, Paphitis’ research stemmed from a community-based organization's concern over the lack of school-aged girls' ability to afford menstrual products. After this concern was expressed, a meeting between university stakeholders was held and a needs assessment was administered across 20 schools in South Africa. Paphitis argues that regardless of the intentions in this project, the researchers perpetuated epistemic injustice. The research was not genuinely participatory and reduced the studies’ participants as sources of data rather than sources of knowledge. In the second case, researchers intentionally embedded community knowledge into every stage of the research process. For example, while creating an interactive workshop session around menstruation, researchers stressed that the social workers they were collaborating with were contributors of knowledge and relied on their expertise in the development of the workshop. Likewise, while developing a community theatre production on menstruation, researchers positioned the high school drama teacher and school learners as co-producers of knowledge. Paphitis argues that while the second case represents a project where community partners were more fully respected as epistemic agents, there was contention amongst her colleagues as to whether it was academically valuable research. The first case, on the other hand, was seen as more valid and interesting to Paphitis’ academic colleagues.
'''Turnhout, Esther, Tamara Metze, Carina Wyborn, Nicole Klenk, and Elena Louder. 2020. “The Politics of Co-Production: Participation, Power, and Transformation.” ''Current Opinion in Environmental Sustainability'', Advancing the science of actionable knowledge for sustainability, 42 (February): 15–21. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cosust.2019.11.009.'''
:Turnhout, Metze, Wyborn, Klenk, and Louder argue that literature on co-production has been largely aspirational and consequently failed to explore how power dynamics shape processes and outcomes. Turnhout et al. argue that the underlying ethic of equality amongst participants in the co-production of knowledge is not self-evident. Literature has indicated that power relationships between participants are uneven from the start, meaning that “elite actors” (i.e., NGOs, governments, scientists) are able to shape the research scope and process. These uneven dynamics are even more pronounced between western and Global South partnerships. These power differentials are concerning because they reproduce existing inequities and impact the legitimacy of the research outcomes. The depoliticization of discourse within research co-production, which may look like elite actors ignoring local realities of power and politics, also reinforces existing inequalities. Turnhout et al. argue that the co-production literature that attempts to address these issues focuses on good processes but fails to address depoliticization. Some studies have explicitly addressed power within co-production projects through a focus on empowerment, however this is less common within studies that understand co-production as a means to “solve” scientific problems. Turnhout et al. argue that humility on the part of elitist actors is essential to negotiating roles and empowering traditionally marginalized voices. When it comes to the impacts of co-production products, there is little literature that indicates the broad societal transformations that are often expected actually occur. Turnhout et al. conclude by asserting there must be a greater recognition of co-production as a political practice that allows for pluralism and the contestations of knowledge claims.
'''Vargas, Carmen, Jill Whelan, Julie Brimblecombe, and Steven Allender. 2022. “Co-Creation, Co-Design, Co-Production for Public Health: A Perspective on Definition and Distinctions.” ''Public Health Research & Practice'' 32 (2). https://apo.org.au/node/318244.'''
:Vargas, Whelan, Brimblecombe, and Allender discuss the differences between co-creation, co-design, and co-production and how to integrate co-production and co-design into public health initiatives. One of the core differences between the three concepts is the point at which diverse stakeholders are brought into the project. Co-creation engages stakeholders from the point of identifying and understanding complex problems through to developing and assessing solutions. Co-design engages stakeholders in developing a solution to an already identified and contextualized problem. Co-production engages stakeholders to implement an already identified solution and a prespecified problem. Vargas et al. argue that since co-design is an instrument for co-creation and co-production is a part of co-creation, co-design and co-production can be considered under the umbrella of co-creation. The authors continue by framing co-creation within participatory action research, emphasizing the important principles of participation, involvement, and engagement for co-creation. They conclude by outlining the six-step continual research cycle of co-creation (identify, analyze, define, design, realize, and evaluate) and highlighting the role co-production and co-design play in these steps.
'''Ward, Paul, Sarah Banks, Angie Hart and Kate Pahl. “Conclusion: Imagining Different Communities and Making Them Happen''.''” In ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'', edited by Sarah Banks, Angie Hart, Kate Pahl, and Paul Ward, 203–10. Bristol University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctv80cccs.16.'''
:Ward et al. conclude ''Co-Producing Research: A Community Development Approach'' by emphasizing the benefits and advantages of co-productive research communities. The authors briefly summarize some of the key challenges of co-production, but ultimately argue that while there may be no co-production project that is completely unproblematic, this should not stop individuals and organizations from engaging in this kind of research.
'''Yep, Kathleen S., and Tania D. Mitchell. 2017. “Decolonizing Community Engagement: Reimagining Service Learning through an Ethnic Studies Lens.” In ''The Cambridge Handbook of Service Learning and Community Engagement'', edited by Corey Dolgon, Tania D. Mitchell, and Timothy K. Eatman, 294–303. Cambridge Handbooks in Psychology. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781316650011.028.'''
:Yep and Mitchell explore how the field of ethnic studies has developed community-based learning through social justice and decolonization frameworks. Yep and Mitchell examine the ethnic studies approach to community-based learning through two case studies of university courses. The first revolved around the course “Grassroots Movements: Immigrant Women, Domestic Workers and Cultural Citizenship” taught at a California research university. The course focused on the domestic workers’ rights movement and emerged to support the California Domestic Worker Bill of Rights. Yep and Mitchell argue that by putting scholarly readings in dialogue with the praxis of activists, students were required to acknowledge domestic workers as analysts in their own right as well as agents. The second case study focused on the course “Globalization and Oceania: Tonga and Hawai’i” which revolved around students working with Tonga community members developing a community archive of cultural materials, like ''ngatu'' and ''koloa'' (gifts exchanged in recognition of important life events), and a voter awareness project around legislation that would benefit the Pacific Islander community. By privileging Tongan knowledge, the course avoided objectifying the community as a lab and rather reinforced the realities of their community partners. Mitchell and Yep argue that unlike other disciplinary approaches to community engagement which centres the student experience, an ethnic studies approach prioritizes the community’s experience. In shifting this focus and adopting a decolonizing approach, power differentials between universities and community partners are redefined. ==Initiatives and Organizations==
'''“Assessing the Practices of Public Scholarship | Imagining America.” 2019. Imagining America | Artists + Scholars in Public Life. October 11, 2019. https://imaginingamerica.org/what-we-do/collaborative-research/assessing-the-practices-of-publicly-engaged-scholars/.'''
:Assessing the Practices of Public Scholarship is a collective for investigating and developing assessment practices for public scholarship and is part of the public scholarship consortium Imagining America. Its work includes developing what they call Democratically Engaged Assessment (DEA), an assessment framework founded upon the idea of democratic civic engagement. This framework seeks to turn assessment of public scholarship into a transformative process involving all stakeholders to analyze collaborative work following six core values: full participation, co-creation, generativity, rigor, practicability, and resilience.
'''“Community-Based Research Canada | Waterloo, Ontario.” n.d. CBRCanada. Accessed July 18, 2022. https://www.communityresearchcanada.ca.'''
:Community-Based Research Canada is a nonprofit, membership-based organization that champions community-based research. It works toward the decolonization of knowledge and against systemic injustice through partnership building, community building, and knowledge mobilization. As of 2023, CBRCanada comprised 61 organizational members, 34 post-secondary institutions, 8 institutes, 19 community organizations, and 150 individual members contributing to community-based research. CBRCanada also organizes courses, workshops, and community of practice events to exchange best practices and network with other members. Their initiatives align with their goals of facilitating connections between individuals, communities and organizations, and championing community-based research.  
'''“Institute for Community Engaged Research: UBC’s Okanagan Campus.” n.d. Accessed July 18, 2022. https://icer.ok.ubc.ca/.'''
:The Institute for Community Engaged Research, located within the University of British Columbia Okanagan, is an interdisciplinary research centre that facilitates community–university relationship building and socially engaged research. Institute members work in various disciplines with a shared commitment to diversity, equity, and social justice. While the members’ research is open-ended, there are five research clusters in this initiative with focused communities of practice: decolonization and Indigeneity, pedagogy, social inclusion, communication of community knowledge, and social, spatial, and economic justice. These activities have the goal of integrating teaching and research into community-engaged relationships, and creating research that promotes equality, equity, and justice at the local, national, and international level.  
'''“UCLA Community Archives Lab – Uplifting Liberatory Memory Work.” n.d. Accessed July 9, 2024. https://communityarchiveslab.ucla.edu/.'''
:The UCLA Community Archives Lab was founded with the intention of exploring the ways that independent, identity-based memory organizations document, shape, and provide access to the histories of minoritized communities, with a particular emphasis on understanding their affective, political, and artistic impact. Additionally, it engages in actions such as teaching and training a new generation of professional archivists in community-engaged and liberatory theories and practices, as well as supporting the autonomy of community archives through collaborative memory work. {{Navigation|previous=Indigenous Knowledges|next=Steps Towards Knowledge Equity}} {{BookCat}}

Engaging Knowledge Diversity/Epistemic I.text:
==Definitions== '''Epistemology''': “It [epistemology] investigates the standards used to assess knowledge or ''why'' we believe what we believe to be true. Far from being the apolitical study of truth, epistemology points to the ways in which power relations shape who is believed and why” (Collins 1990). '''Epistemic injustice''': “A wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower” (Fricker 2007). It includes “a wide range of topics concerning wrongful treatment and unjust structures in meaning-making and knowledge producing practices, such as the following: exclusion and silencing; invisibility and inaudibility (or distorted presence or representation); having one’s meanings or contributions systematically distorted, misheard, or misrepresented; having diminished status or standing in communicative practices” (Kidd, Medina, and Pohlhaus 2017). '''Discriminatory epistemic injustice''': “A wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower” as a result of identity prejudice (subcategories: testimonial injustice, hermeneutical injustice, and contributory injustice) (Nikolaidis 2021, referencing Fricker 2007). '''Testimonial injustice''': “A wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower” and speaker when a hearer perceives them to have less credibility than they would have otherwise due to ethically unsound reasons, usually identity prejudices (Steers-McCrum 2020, referencing Fricker 2007). '''Testimonial justice''': When the degree of credibility that a person is afforded is aligned with the degree of evidence that they are stating the truth (Steers-McCrum 2020, referencing Fricker 2007). '''Testimonial smothering (or ''coerced silencing)''''': An injustice that occurs when a speaker truncates or silences their testimony due to the perception that the audience will be unwilling or unable to listen to and/or be receptive to it, which would lead to misconceptions that could contribute to harm (Lee 2021, referencing Dotson 2011). '''Hermeneutical injustice''': A wrong done to a person when their lived or social experience is excluded from collective knowledge due to prejudice (Nikolaidis 2021, referencing Fricker 2007). '''Contributory injustice (also referred to as ''third-order epistemic injustice'')''': When an individual willfully refuses to acknowledge marginalized knowledge and as a result minimizes a knower’s ability to contribute to an epistemic community and diminishes that knower’s epistemic agency (Nikolaidis 2021, referencing Dotson). '''Distributive epistemic injustice''': The unjust distribution of epistemic goods such as education or access to expert information (Coady, 2010). ==Resources== ===Core Concepts and Debates===
'''Albornoz, Denisse, Angela Okune, and Leslie Chan. 2020. “Can Open Scholarly Practices Redress Epistemic Injustice?” In ''Reassembling Scholarly Communications: Histories, Infrastructures, and Global Politics of Open Access'', edited by Martin Paul Eve and Jonathan Gray, 65–79''.'' Cambridge: MIT Press. https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/11885.003.0009.'''
:Albornoz, Okune, and Chan challenge the idea that open access has made all knowledge more available. Rather, the authors suggest, open access has made research undertaken by scholars in the Global North more available, to the detriment and increased obscuration of research by scholars in the Global South. Albornoz, Okune, and Chan reinforce this point when they argue that “open systems may potentially replicate the very values and power imbalances that the movement initially sought to change” (65), especially the replication of ''epistemic injustice'', or “the devaluing of someone’s knowledge or capacity as a knower” (65). The authors also outline institutional forces that have invalidated certain types of knowledge, including academic publishing, the primacy of the English language, and professional advancement criteria. Albornoz, Okune, and Chan conclude by making four recommendations for open research: 1) for scholars in the Global North to recognize their privilege; 2) to challenge the current standards and norms that promote epistemic injustice; 3) to learn from ongoing projects that are already seeking to address injustice; and 4) to recontextualize open access as a more radical movement with direct responsibility for undoing structural oppression.
'''Altanian, Melanie, and Nadja El Kassar. 2021. “Epistemic Injustice and Collective Wrongdoing: Introduction to Special Issue.” ''Social Epistemology'' 35 (2): 99–108. https://doi.org/10.1080/02691728.2020.1843199.'''
:Rather than focusing on epistemic injustice as it affects individuals, the authors in this special issue examine epistemic injustice primarily as a collective or group phenomenon. Altanian and El Kassar situate their own introduction, and each of the issue’s subsequent contributions, in relation to existing scholarship, citing the theoretical work of Kristie Dotson, Gaile Pohlhaus Jr., José Medina, Amandine Catala, and Katharine Jenkins—all critics they laud for fruitfully extending Miranda Fricker’s foundational 2007 study. In the process, they identify and elucidate three of the special issue’s noteworthy themes, beginning with “the effects of epistemic injustice and collective wrongdoing.” They contend that most of these effects impact both individuals and collectives; however, they add that the harmful consequences of epistemic injustice can also be observed in “dispersed groups, such as survivors of rape and sexual violence” (102). Next, they turn to the issue’s second major theme: the structural or systemic origins of epistemic injustice. Exploring this theme in reference to concepts such as “hermeneutical marginalization” and “hermeneutical domination,” they emphasize the rhetorical and material importance of ignorance to those who have historically perpetuated—or continue to perpetuate—epistemic injustice: “Such ignorance is both generated and sustained by individual and institutional agents and structures with the aim to maintain an unjust status quo. Hence, they signify not only states but ''practices'' of ignorance” (104; emphasis added). The third and final theme identified by Altanian and El Kassar, “Remedies and Resistance,” underscores several possible responses to this practice of ignorance and to the harmful effects of epistemic injustice in its many other forms. Most notably, perhaps, they posit “intellectual self-trust” as an antidote to the kinds of intellectual gaslighting they associate with epistemic injustice at the individual as well as group level.
'''Anderson, Elizabeth. 2012. “Epistemic Justice as a Virtue of Social Institutions.” ''Social Epistemology'' 26 (2): 163–73. https://doi.org/10.1080/02691728.2011.652211.'''
:Anderson stresses the importance of structural remedies to epistemic injustice, as a friendly amendment to Miranda Fricker’s discussion of virtue-based remedies (see Fricker 2007). Anderson argues that Fricker’s attention to virtue-based remedies is lacking for two main reasons. First, virtue-based remedies require those perpetuating injustice to become aware of dissonances between their explicit beliefs and unconscious stereotypes and practice critical reflection, which Anderson argues is unrealistic and impractical. Second, virtue-based remedies fail to address the structural forms of testimonial injustice. Anderson identifies three structural causes for prejudicial credibility deficits: differential access to the markers of credibility, ethnocentrism, and shared reality bias. These causes become problematic when they fall along boundaries of systematic inequality, and they require structural remedies, such as genuine school integration.
'''Anderson, Luvell. 2017. “Epistemic Injustice and the Philosophy of Race.” In ''The Routledge Handbook of Epistemic Injustice'', edited by Ian James Kidd, José Medina, and Gaile Pohlhaus, 139–48. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315212043.'''
:Anderson discusses the ways post-racialism produces hermeneutical injustice. Anderson outlines two notions of post-racialism: descriptive and prescriptive. Descriptive post-racialism asserts that we are currently in a state where race no longer matters economically, politically, or socially; this is demonstrably false. Prescriptive post-racialism is about the future realization of an ideal role of race. This ideal takes four forms: assimilationism, eliminativism, colour-blindness, and post-racism. Anderson outlines two types of hermeneutical injustice related to these ideas of post-racialism: illocutionary flipping, where the meaning of a speech act is interpreted as opposite or flipped due to the speaker’s marginalized social identity, such as their gender or race (e.g., a woman saying no to sexual advances and this being interpreted as a yes), and silencing, where a speech act is denied its performative power (e.g., a no is simply disregarded). Post-racialism contributes to hermeneutical gaps, where racial identity is no longer acknowledged, but remains influential in people’s lived experience. This gap contributes to illocutionary flipping and silencing: Anderson gives the example of “Black lives matter” being interpreted as “only Black lives matter” rather than its intended meaning of “Black lives also matter.” Anderson concludes that the post-racial ideal entrenches disharmony and widens the hermeneutical gaps that make harmony more difficult to attain.
'''Byskov, Morten Fibieger. 2021. “What Makes Epistemic Injustice an ‘Injustice’?” ''Journal of Social Philosophy'' 52, (1): 114–31. https://doi.org/10.1111/josp.12348.'''
:Byskov shifts the focus of epistemic injustice studies from what qualifies it as epistemic to what qualifies it as injustice. He suggests there are five conditions that are central to evaluating claims of epistemic injustice, including two drawn from Miranda Fricker’s work (see Fricker 2007). The disadvantage condition requires that a person be disadvantaged directly or indirectly in their capacity as a knower, and the prejudice condition requires that the disadvantage must be based on characteristics irrelevant to their capacity as a knower (e.g., ethnicity, gender, social background). Byskov also describes three additional conditions: the stakeholder condition requires that a person have a direct stake in the matter at hand, the epistemic condition requires that the person possess relevant knowledge, and the social justice condition requires that the person also suffers from other social injustices. Byskov argues that each of the five conditions are only partial and that meeting any one of them does not necessarily constitute an epistemic injustice. The set of conditions should not be taken as binary; rather, they should be applied as a scale where the more conditions that are violated, the greater the injustice. Byskov’s conditions provide a framework for evaluating potential epistemic injustices.
'''Carmona, Carla. 2021. “Silencing by Not Telling: Testimonial Void as a New Kind of Testimonial Injustice.” ''Social Epistemology'' 35 (6): 577–92. https://doi.org/10.1080/02691728.2021.1887395.'''
:Carmona argues that testimonial void is a newly classified testimonial injustice. Testimonial void occurs when a speaker withholds their testimony based on epistemically and ethically faulty beliefs that a would-be-hearer cannot do anything epistemically relevant with it; that is, they cannot contextualize the information well enough to understand it or act on it. In cases of testimonial void, speakers withhold epistemic material based on prejudicial assessments of a hearer-to-be’s epistemic capacity. Being deprived of epistemic inputs, the hearer-to-be’s capacity to engage in epistemic practices is significantly diminished, and the cycle of exclusion may indirectly lead to them being silenced. Unlike traditional cases of testimonial injustice, in cases of testimonial void it is not a speaker’s credibility that is assessed based on prejudice. Rather, the potential hearer’s epistemic aptness— their ability to be a hearer— is assessed in a biased manner. Since testimonial void is based on judgements of epistemic aptness where little evidence of an individual’s actual competence may be present for a speaker’s judgment, Carmona argues that testimonial void illuminates the need for epistemic equality trust. This kind of trust maintains that individuals have an obligation to trust others as receivers and contributors of epistemic materials by virtue of their being human.
'''Coady, David. 2010. “Two Concepts of Epistemic Injustice.” ''Episteme'' 7 (2): 101–13. https://doi.org/10.3366/E1742360010000845.'''
:Coady compares two concepts of epistemic injustice. The first one, based on a critique of Alvin Goldman’s “veritistic social epistemology,” refers to the unjust ignorance or error about something a person should know or be right about. The second and most employed concept, as defined by Miranda Fricker, refers to an unjust deficit in credibility or intelligibility. While both forms of injustice are often systematic and oppress people with relatively little social power, Coady argues that there is a tension between the two concepts because if a powerless group is ignorant or in error about an issue, then they will be deemed less credible. To resolve this tension, the author proposes distinguishing the types of propositions in relation to which people face epistemic injustice. Unjust ignorance or error tends to involve propositions about how oppressed people can become more socially empowered, while unjust credibility or intelligibility deficits usually relate to propositions about a person’s own experiences. Although both categories may overlap, Coady states that more work can be done to resolve the tensions between the two forms of epistemic injustice.
'''Cohen, Noa, and Mirko Daniel Garasic. 2024. “Informed Ignorance as a Form of Epistemic Injustice.” ''Philosophies'' 9 (3): 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/philosophies9030059.'''
:Cohen and Garasic explore the harms caused by information malpractices from an epistemic perspective, introducing the concept of "informed ignorance." This term refers to a condition where individuals are exposed to a vast amount of information but lack relevant knowledge, a phenomenon exacerbated by technological advancements and social media. The authors argue that this discrepancy between knowledge and information fosters misinformation and perpetuates epistemic injustices, such as marginalizing certain viewpoints and reinforcing unjust knowledge hierarchies. They also define rational ignorance, in which complex or lengthy information becomes inaccessible, contributing to the problem of informed ignorance. The impact of informed ignorance includes decision-making based on biased information, which can lead to discriminatory practices and human rights violations. The authors emphasize the importance of prioritizing verified information on social media platforms and propose both theoretical and practical solutions to combat epistemic injustices, such as focusing on the practical consequences of knowledge, ensuring rigorous and transparent scientific research practices, promoting media literacy, fostering intellectual virtues like open-mindedness, and encouraging ethical practices in science and media communication. The authors conclude by emphasizing the importance of understanding and addressing the forces driving epistemic injustice. They suggest that informed ignorance may stem from a counterculture against intellectual elites, which diminishes the value of their work while fostering skepticism and mistrust. To combat informed ignorance and its negative consequences, Cohen and Garasic call for actions grounded in robust theoretical principles and clear epistemic virtues, aimed at supporting a well-informed and enlightened society.
'''Collins, Patricia Hill. 2017. “Intersectionality and Epistemic Injustice.” In ''The Routledge Handbook of Epistemic Injustice'', edited by Ian James Kidd, José Medina, and Gaile Pohlhaus, 115–24. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315212043.'''
:Collins examines how the transformation of the concept of intersectionality within academia illuminates epistemic injustice. Collins focuses on two primary forms of epistemic injustice: (1) the epistemic injustices that intersectional approaches seek to address and (2) the epistemic injustices carried out against scholars who claim intersectionality. Collins argues that Kimberlé Crenshaw’s positioning of intersectionality within the dynamic border between activism and academic politics has been overlooked, while intersectionality’s origins within academia has remained in focus. As a result of the pressure of the academy, actors involved in social movements and academia were coerced to develop a depoliticized version of intersectionality that was divorced from its roots in social activism. Collins asserts that casting identity politics and standpoint epistemology as limited and biased ways of knowing undermines the epistemic agency of oppressed peoples. Casting identity politics and standpoint epistemology as inferior forms of knowledge, while embracing a depoliticized version of intersectionality, constitutes a misrecognition of Crenshaw’s work, epistemic violence, and suppresses the radical potential of more-unruly intersectionality. This misrecognition occurred primarily through testimonial quieting and smothering (see, e.g., Dotson 2011). Collins concludes by emphasizing the persistent work needed to challenge epistemic injustice within epistemic practices.
'''Dotson, Kristie. 2011. “Tracking Epistemic Violence, Tracking Practices of Silencing.” ''Hypatia'' 26 (2): 236–57. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1527-2001.2011.01177.x.'''
:Dotson identifies two practices of silencing that occur due to epistemic violence, understood as the “failure of an audience to communicatively reciprocate, either intentionally or unintentionally, in linguistic exchanges owning to pernicious ignorance” (242). The first practice of silencing is testimonial quieting, which happens when an audience does not recognize a speaker as a knower, usually due to stereotypes or prejudice. The second practice is testimonial smothering, which occurs when a speaker truncates their risky testimony, selecting only content for which the audience demonstrates testimonial competence. Dotson draws from the work of feminist scholars Patricia Hill Collins and Kimberlé Crenshaw to illustrate how women of color often face both forms of silencing. Identifying these practices removes the burden from the speaker to prove the existence of silencing when attempting to testify from an oppressed position in society.
'''Dotson, Kristie. 2014. “Conceptualizing Epistemic Oppression.” ''Social Epistemology'' 28 (2): 115–38. https://doi.org/10.1080/02691728.2013.782585.'''
:Dotson examines the concept of epistemic oppression, understood as a “persistent […] exclusion that hinders one’s contribution to knowledge production” (115), to distinguish in which cases epistemic oppression cannot be reduced to social and political forms of oppression. Extending Plato’s Allegory of the cave, the author distinguishes between reducible epistemic oppression and irreducible epistemic oppression, which differ in their resistance to change. Reducible epistemic oppression can be addressed through epistemic resources within the same epistemological system, so they are primarily caused by social and historical factors. Irreducible epistemic oppression is addressed by recognizing the limits of the epistemological system (social imaginaries), so it requires an immense change. Dotson concludes that this distinction between reducible and irreducible epistemic oppression can clarify when it is apt to use the concept of epistemic oppression without reducing it to social or political oppression.
'''Fricker, Miranda. 2007. ''Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing''. ''Epistemic Injustice''. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198237907.001.0001.'''
:Fricker coins and explores the term ''epistemic injustice'' as an injustice specifically associated with one’s knowledge-based experience, within a context of social power''.'' Fricker’s definition of the term is “a wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower” (1). Epistemic injustice is two-pronged, according to Fricker, as it can take the form of ''testimonial injustice''—where a speaker is discredited due to the hearer’s prejudice—or ''hermeneutical injustice''—where a broader social misunderstanding or conceptual gap puts a speaker at a disadvantage. Fricker’s overarching goal in exploring this topic is to reveal the ethical aspects of general / routine epistemic practices: sharing what one knows and making sense of social experiences and interactions.
'''Grasswick, Heidi. 2018. “Understanding Epistemic Trust Injustices and Their Harms.” ''Royal Institute of Philosophy Supplements'' 84 (November): 69–91. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1358246118000553.'''
:Grasswick argues that to fully understand epistemic injustice we must focus not only on people's ability to be contributors of knowledge, but also their capacity to take up knowledge. Grasswick analyzes the process of taking up knowledge through the lens of epistemic trust. Grasswick states there are two conditions of trust: competence (how confident a person can be that an expert is capable of being a provider of significant knowledge) and sincerity/care (how confident a person can be that an expert will act in their epistemic interests). When the (dis)trust is between an individual and an institution, the trustworthiness of the institution’s practices, as opposed to the trustworthiness of the individuals within the institution, is important. In cases of epistemic trust injustice, a marginalized person cannot reasonably trust an expert or community of experts due to past interactions. As a result, the marginalized person's ability to attain knowledge is minimized, as is their epistemic agency. Grasswick discusses epistemic trust injustices in relation to the scientific community, noting that these injustices can have particularly harmful effects on marginalized people, such as when the medical institution is perceived as untrustworthy. To address epistemic trust injustice, there must be a commitment from institutions to change epistemic practices and create more inclusive communities of practitioners.
'''Kidd, Ian James, José Medina, and Gaile M. Pohlhaus, eds. 2017. ''The Routledge Handbook of Epistemic Injustice''. Routledge Handbooks in Philosophy. Routledge, Taylor & Francis Group. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315212043.'''
:This collection, which consists of an introduction and thirty-seven individual chapters, provides an overview of concepts, issues, and case studies relevant to the topic of epistemic injustice. In their introduction, Kidd, Medina, and Pohlhaus Jr. stress the timeliness of such discussions, with attention to the kinds of considerations that have animated scholarship and scholarly communication in recent years: :In the era of information and communication, issues of misinformation and miscommunication are more pressing than ever. Who has voice and who doesn’t? Are voices interacting with equal agency and power? In whose terms are they communicating? Who is being understood and who isn’t (and at what cost)? Who is being believed? And who is even being acknowledged and engaged with? (1) :With these questions in mind, the editors go on to explain the significance of epistemic injustice in terms of its intersection with historical and current discussions in philosophy, its embeddedness in larger sociocultural and intellectual developments, and its widespread presence across a variety of individual or localized contexts. Each of the subsequent chapters—organized into five sections—touches on one or more of these points of connection. ''Part 1: Core concepts'' defines key terms; ''Part 2: Liberatory epistemologies and axes of oppression'' situates the concept of epistemic injustice in relation to historical intellectual traditions; ''Part 3: Schools of thought and subfields within epistemology'' explores specific subfields and their methodological approaches to the subject; ''Part 4: Socio-political, ethical, and psychological dimensions of knowing'' digs deeper into the interdisciplinary manifestations and critical applications of epistemic injustice; and ''Part V: Case studies of epistemic injustice'' illustrates the foregoing discussions with reference to noteworthy cases.
'''Lagewaard, T. J. 2021. “Epistemic Injustice and Deepened Disagreement.” ''Philosophical Studies'' 178 (5): 1571–92. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11098-020-01496-x.'''
:Lagewaard argues that everyday arguments can become deep disagreements about epistemic principles as a result of pre-existing epistemic injustice, proposing that when epistemic injustice manifests itself in ordinary disagreements, the disagreement shifts from the initial topic to what gets to count as evidence. Lagewaard conceptualizes deep disagreement on a scale: disagreements about fundamental epistemic principles (e.g., the reliability of sense perception) constitute the deepest kind of disagreement, and those about derived epistemic principles (e.g., the reliability of methods in biology) constitute less deep forms. Lagewaard illustrates this argument by discussing the public disagreement in Dutch society around whether the figure “Black Pete” is racist. Those who experience racial oppression are at an epistemic advantage when discussing the significance of racism, but identity prejudice can cause dominant groups to disregard their testimony or not give it proper weight. In this case, testimonial injustice contributes to propositional disagreements: disagreement about whether Black Pete perpetuates racism becomes deep disagreement about whose testimony counts as evidence. Hermeneutical injustice also contributes to deep disagreement. When there is minimal uptake of epistemic resources created by oppressed groups and consequently a lack of shared epistemic concepts, dominant groups will disregard non-dominant groups’ testimony as nonsensical. Lagewaard concludes by arguing that testimonial and hermeneutical injustice are mutually reinforcing: when concepts do not align with the understandings of dominant groups, they are unlikely to count the testimony of non-dominant individuals as evidence and dismiss their arguments as overreactions.
'''Lee, J. Y. 2021. “Anticipatory Epistemic Injustice.” ''Social Epistemology'' 35 (6): 564–76. https://doi.org/10.1080/02691728.2021.1924306.'''
:Lee proposes there is a kind of epistemic injustice–anticipatory epistemic injustice–that does not fit into the models advanced by Miranda Fricker or Kristie Dotson. Lee defines anticipatory epistemic injustice as the wrongs a person experiences as a result of the anticipated challenges to their testimony. For example, a person may decide not to share their religious experiences because they anticipate that their experiences will not be taken seriously given negative prejudices around religious groups. Anticipatory epistemic injustice is distinct from Dotson’s concept of testimonial smothering because it does not require an incompetent audience. The wrong occurs because people are placed into this position of epistemic precarity unjustly and accordingly relinquish the more authoritative testimonial approaches available to others. Lee argues that anticipatory epistemic injustice can occur at the personal, interpersonal, and structural level and identifies two types of anticipatory epistemic injustice: transparent and opaque. In transparent cases, epistemic agents self-silence or distort testimony for explicit reasons; the decision to disclose experiences is part of a cost-benefit analysis of expected outcomes. In opaque cases, agents distort their testimony without being aware of the forces that have led to this anticipatory behaviour. Lee concludes by asserting that anticipatory epistemic injustice is particularly harmful because it can take so many forms and because it can occur in cases where the threat is real or merely perceived.
'''McKinnon, Rachel. 2017. “Allies Behaving Badly: Gaslighting as Epistemic Injustice.” In ''The Routledge Handbook of Epistemic Injustice'', edited by Ian James Kidd, José Medina, and Gaile Pohlhaus, 167–74. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315212043.'''
:McKinnon explores the bad epistemic practices of allies from a “trans* perspective,” a term McKinnon uses to denote maximal inclusivity. These include epistemic gaslighting, where listeners cast doubt that the harm a speaker claims occurred actually happened as described. Epistemic gaslighting and its features are illustrated through a fictional series of events between three co-workers, Victoria (a trans woman), James, and Susan. At an office party, James mispronouns Victoria, which has happened repeatedly in the past. Victoria voices her concerns about this to Susan, who claims she must have misheard James and reminds Victoria that James is an ally. McKinnon argues that this example of epistemic gaslighting fits within Fricker’s framework of testimonial injustice for two reasons. First, the stereotype of trans women being overly emotional and thus irrational is at play when Susan dismisses Victoria’s account of James’ behaviour. Second, Susan questions Victoria’s testimony based on James’ identity as an ally. Allies gaslighting marginally situated knowers is an especially harmful form of testimonial injustice because it betrays the epistemic and moral trust the speakers have given them. Due to their positionality, the testimony of trans people and other marginally situated knowers should be given more epistemic weight and credibility. Allies should decentre their own perceptions and trust the testimony of marginalized people. McKinnon argues we should abandon the concept of “ally” in favor of active bystanders; those who appropriately intercede when they see discrimination or harassment take place.
'''Mitova, Veli. 2024. “Can Theorising Epistemic Injustice Help Us Decolonise?” ''Inquiry,'' 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1080/0020174X.2024.2327489.'''
:Mitova contends that tools from critical race, queer, and feminist theory can significantly contribute to theorizing epistemic decolonization. She addresses concerns about the liberatory potential of epistemic injustice scholarship due to the belief that "epistemic injustice is white-people stuff" (WPS). She proposes three perspectives for explaining why epistemic injustice is considered WPS: the rhetoric of beginnings, which refers to the appropriation of concepts developed by Black feminists; institutional incorporation, where concepts from resistant epistemologies become institutionalized and lose their emancipatory potential; and the endemically marginalizing perspective of epistemic injustice, which focuses on the oppressor’s viewpoint rather than the perspective of the oppressed. However, she believes that these challenges can be surmounted, for example, by studying epistemic oppression, white ignorance, and contributory injustice. Epistemic oppression, understood as a persistent infringement on one's ability to utilize shared epistemic resources, provides a possible rationale for recentering the knowledge enterprise as a means of epistemic decolonization to reclaim the ability to theorise from one’s own location. White ignorance, defined as a non-knowing where race plays a causal role, can help explain the prevalence of epistemically colonized attitudes, and the resistance to decolonising. Finally, contributory injustice occurs when marginalized epistemic resources are disregarded by dominant knowers, preventing them from influencing the mainstream knowledge economy. This active ignorance by the colonizer strips marginalized groups of their epistemic authority and undermines their capacity to exercise their epistemic agency effectively. By employing these concepts, Mitova argues that we can work towards more ethical and effective tools for addressing epistemic injustice and advancing the goals of decolonization.
'''Nikolaidis, A. C. 2021. “A Third Conception of Epistemic Injustice.” ''Studies in Philosophy and Education'' 40 (4): 381–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11217-021-09760-1.'''
:Nikolaidis discusses formative epistemic injustice, which he argues is distinct from Miranda Fricker’s standard conceptions of discriminatory epistemic injustice and distributive epistemic injustice. The source of epistemic formative injustice is not discrimination or maldistribution but “malformation”: the unjustified restriction of one’s formative capacities such that possibilities are foreclosed. There is both an agentive component (deriving from brainwashing or manipulation from external forces) and a structural component (caused by social conditions) of formative epistemic injustice. Additionally, Nikolaidis identifies two categories of harm resulting from formative epistemic injustice: formative harm (harm to a person’s capacity as knower) and practical harm (material harm). Central to Nikolaidis’ definition is that this type of injustice impacts both privileged and marginalized groups. When epistemic resources originating from non-dominant groups are marginalized, the development of privileged and marginalized groups as knowers is impeded, even if the nature of the impediment is different. Formative epistemic injustice can also occur even when epistemic resources are evenly distributed: just because marginalized students have access to high-quality educational resources, that does not guarantee they will experience epistemic justice. Nikolaidis concludes by arguing that formative epistemic injustice is especially harmful for children, who are vulnerable to malformation.
'''Steers-McCrum, Alex R. 2020. “Don’t Put Words in My Mouth: Self-Appointed Speaking-for Is Testimonial Injustice Without Prejudice.” ''Social Epistemology'' 34 (3): 241–52. https://doi.org/10.1080/02691728.2019.1682710.'''
:Steers-McCrum argues that self-appointed speaking-for–in which a speaker speaks for a person or group who has not authorized them to do so–is a case of testimonial injustice as advanced by Miranda Fricker. Steers-McCrum argues that self-appointed speaking-for and testimonial injustice share the same epistemic harm: both wrong an individual in their capacity to be a giver of knowledge. Where self-appointed speaking-for and Fricker’s testimonial injustice diverge is the requirement of prejudicial attitudes. For a communicative act to count as testimonial injustice, a person’s failure to attribute appropriate credibility to a speaker must be based on prejudicial attitudes. Self-appointed speaking-for does not require the presence of prejudicial attitudes for it to be unjust because the practice is wrong by its very nature. Through speaking for someone, an individual demonstrates they do not have confidence in the epistemic capabilities of a would-be speaker to share their own experiences and in turn prevent the would-be speaker from gaining credibility through their speech. Regardless of the individual’s intentions, speaking-for another person stunts their epistemic agency and by its nature is wrong. Steers-McCrum concludes, arguing that understanding self-appointed speaking-for as an epistemic wrong expands the concept of testimonial injustice beyond only cases where prejudice is involved. Steers-McCrum also emphasizes that self-appointed speaking-for is not just a minor epistemic infraction, it is a serious epistemic wrong that perpetuates other forms of injustice.
